parts.label: a
parts.text:
A solution of an unknown salt is tested. Aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess to give a colourless solution. Aqueous ammonia gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. Which cation is present?
A Al³⁺
B Ca²⁺
C Zn²⁺
D Cr³⁺
parts.answer: A Al³⁺
parts.working: Al³⁺: white ppt soluble in excess NaOH(aq), insoluble in excess NH₃(aq). Zn²⁺ is wrong because its white ppt also dissolves in excess ammonia; Ca²⁺ ppt does not dissolve in excess NaOH; Cr³⁺ gives a green ppt.

practice.stem: Four gases, A to D, are collected in test-tubes during practical work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gas A relights a glowing splint. Identify gas A.
parts.answer: Oxygen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Gas B turns damp red litmus paper blue. Identify gas B.
parts.answer: Ammonia

parts.label: c
parts.text: Gas C bleaches damp litmus paper. Identify gas C.
parts.answer: Chlorine

parts.label: d
parts.text: Gas D turns acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless. Identify gas D.
parts.answer: Sulfur dioxide

parts.label: e
parts.text: Describe the test for carbon dioxide and its positive result.
parts.answer: Bubble the gas through limewater; limewater turns milky.

practice.stem:
A student in a Lahore school laboratory tests a blue-green solid X dissolved in water.
Test 1: flame test — blue-green flame.
Test 2: aqueous sodium hydroxide added dropwise then in excess — light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess.
Test 3: aqueous ammonia added dropwise then in excess — light blue precipitate, which dissolves in excess to give a dark blue solution.
Test 4: dilute nitric acid added, then aqueous silver nitrate — white precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the cation in X. Give one observation from the table that supports your answer.
parts.answer: Copper(II) ion, Cu²⁺; e.g. light blue precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia to give a dark blue solution (or blue-green flame).
parts.working: B1 Cu²⁺/copper(II); B1 one correct supporting observation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the anion in X.
parts.answer: Chloride ion, Cl⁻.
parts.working: B1 white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dilute nitric acid, and not dilute hydrochloric acid, is used to acidify the solution in test 4.
parts.answer: Hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions, which would themselves give a white precipitate with silver nitrate, so a false positive result.
parts.working: M1 HCl adds Cl⁻ ions; A1 these would give a white ppt whatever X contained.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest the formula of X.
parts.answer: CuCl₂

practice.stem: A student collects a colourless liquid from a well near Mithi in the Thar desert and wants to know whether it is water and whether it is pure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a chemical test that shows the liquid contains water. Give the result.
parts.answer: Add anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: it turns from white to blue (or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride: blue to pink).
parts.working: B1 reagent; B1 colour change both colours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The chemical test does not show that the water is pure. Describe a physical test that would show whether the water is pure.
parts.answer: Measure its boiling point (or melting point): pure water boils at exactly 100 °C (melts at 0 °C) at normal pressure.
parts.working: B1 boiling/melting point; B1 correct value 100 °C / 0 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The well water boils at 101.5 °C. What does this tell you about it?
parts.answer: It is impure; it contains dissolved substances.

practice.stem:
Solution Y contains one cation and one anion.
Test 1: aqueous sodium hydroxide added — green precipitate, insoluble in excess.
Test 2: the mixture from test 1 is warmed — no gas that affects damp red litmus paper.
Test 3: aluminium foil is added to the warm mixture — a gas is produced that turns damp red litmus paper blue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the cation in Y. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Iron(II), Fe²⁺: green precipitate with NaOH(aq) that does not dissolve in excess.
parts.working: B1 Fe²⁺; B1 green ppt insoluble in excess.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the anion in Y.
parts.answer: Nitrate, NO₃⁻
parts.working: B1 ammonia produced only when aluminium is present.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why test 2 was needed before the result of test 3 could be used.
parts.answer: Ammonium ions also give ammonia when warmed with NaOH(aq); test 2 shows no ammonium ions are present, so the ammonia in test 3 must come from reduction of nitrate by aluminium.
parts.working: M1 NH₄⁺ gives ammonia with warm NaOH; A1 test 2 rules out NH₄⁺ so ammonia comes from nitrate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest what the student would see if the green precipitate in test 1 was left to stand in air for some time.
parts.answer: It turns orange-brown / red-brown at the surface (iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III)).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which reagent can be used to tell aqueous sodium sulfite apart from aqueous sodium sulfate?
A dilute nitric acid followed by aqueous barium nitrate
B acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII)
C aqueous sodium hydroxide
D a flame test
parts.answer: B acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII)
parts.working: Sulfite ions decolourise acidified potassium manganate(VII) (purple to colourless); sulfate ions do not. A is wrong because nitric acid oxidises sulfite to sulfate, so both would give a white precipitate; C and D give the same result for both (both contain Na⁺).

practice.stem: A technician in Peshawar has four unlabelled bottles of colourless solution. She knows they are zinc chloride, aluminium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using aqueous ammonia only, describe how the technician could tell the zinc chloride solution from the aluminium chloride solution. Give the result for each.
parts.answer: Add aqueous ammonia dropwise then in excess to each. Both give a white precipitate. With zinc chloride the precipitate dissolves in excess to give a colourless solution; with aluminium chloride the precipitate does not dissolve.
parts.working: M1 dropwise then excess; A1 Zn²⁺ white ppt soluble in excess; A1 Al³⁺ white ppt insoluble in excess.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the technician could tell the potassium bromide solution from the potassium iodide solution. Give the result for each.
parts.answer: Acidify with dilute nitric acid and add aqueous silver nitrate. Bromide gives a cream precipitate; iodide gives a yellow precipitate.
parts.working: B1 acidify with dilute nitric acid + silver nitrate; B1 cream for bromide; B1 yellow for iodide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a test that would show that the potassium solutions both contain potassium ions. Give the result.
parts.answer: Flame test: lilac flame.

practice.stem: A student investigates how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of its reaction with marble chips. She collects the carbon dioxide over water in an upturned measuring cylinder and records the volume every 30 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the measuring cylinder is not a good way to measure the volume of gas.
parts.answer: Some carbon dioxide dissolves in the water / gas escapes before the bung is replaced / the readings are hard to read accurately while the cylinder is in the water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a piece of apparatus that would give more accurate measurements of the gas volume.
parts.answer: Gas syringe

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student should use the same mass of marble chips each time.
parts.answer: Only one variable (the concentration of acid) should be changed so that the test is fair; more marble would change the volume of gas / rate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student should repeat each experiment.
parts.answer: To check the results are reliable / to identify anomalous results and calculate an average.

practice.stem: A student investigates how temperature affects the time taken for a cross drawn on paper under a flask to disappear when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to aqueous sodium thiosulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable.
parts.answer: Temperature of the sodium thiosulfate solution

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Time for the cross to disappear

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any two of: volume of thiosulfate; concentration of thiosulfate; volume of acid; concentration of acid; same flask/cross; same observer.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the student could keep the solution at a steady temperature.
parts.answer: Use a (thermostatically controlled) water-bath.

practice.stem: Rock salt from a mine in the Salt Range contains sodium chloride mixed with insoluble rock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to find the percentage by mass of insoluble impurities in a sample of crushed rock salt. You may use common laboratory apparatus, including an electronic balance and an oven.
parts.answer: Weigh, dissolve, filter, wash and dry the residue, weigh, calculate.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: weigh a known mass of rock salt (e.g. 10.0 g) on a balance; add to a beaker of water and stir (warm) until all the salt has dissolved; weigh a filter paper; filter the mixture; wash the residue with a little distilled water to remove salt solution; dry the residue and paper in an oven (or warm place) and weigh; repeat drying and weighing until mass is constant; mass of impurity = mass of dried paper + residue − mass of paper; % = mass of impurity ÷ mass of rock salt × 100.

practice.stem: A student measures the temperature change when 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid is mixed with 25 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide in a glass beaker.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a polystyrene cup is better than a glass beaker for this experiment.
parts.answer: Polystyrene is a poor conductor of heat (insulator), so less heat is lost to the surroundings and the temperature rise measured is larger / more accurate.
parts.working: M1 insulator / less heat loss; A1 temperature change nearer the true value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one further improvement to reduce heat loss. Explain why it is an improvement.
parts.answer: Put a lid on the cup — this reduces heat lost by convection/evaporation from the surface.
parts.working: B1 lid (or stand cup in a beaker / lag it); B1 reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student uses a measuring cylinder to measure 25 cm³ of acid. Suggest a more accurate piece of apparatus and explain why it is an improvement.
parts.answer: A volumetric pipette (or burette); it measures a fixed volume more accurately / smaller uncertainty.

practice.stem: A student in a Karachi college compares the energy released by burning two liquid fuels, ethanol and propan-1-ol. Each fuel is burned in a spirit burner under a copper can containing water, and the temperature rise of the water is measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two variables that must be kept the same to make this a fair comparison.
parts.answer: Any two of: volume (mass) of water; distance from flame to can; starting temperature of water; temperature rise / time of heating; same can; same burner design.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The temperature rise measured is much smaller than expected from data books. Suggest two reasons.
parts.answer: Heat lost to the surroundings/air; heat used to warm the can; incomplete combustion (soot); evaporation of fuel from the wick.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the student finds the mass of fuel burned.
parts.answer: Weigh the spirit burner (with cap) before and after heating; subtract.

practice.stem: Antacid tablets are sold in many pharmacies in Pakistan. Three brands, P, Q and R, each claim to relieve indigestion by neutralising stomach acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to find which brand of antacid tablet neutralises the most hydrochloric acid per tablet. You are provided with dilute hydrochloric acid of known concentration, methyl orange indicator and common laboratory apparatus. Each tablet is an insoluble base.
parts.answer: Direct titration: titrate one crushed tablet of each brand (in water with methyl orange) with the hydrochloric acid from a burette; the brand needing the largest volume of acid neutralises the most.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: crush one tablet of brand 1 and place in a conical flask with water / measured volume of distilled water; add a few drops of methyl orange; fill a burette with the hydrochloric acid and record the initial reading; add acid from the burette while swirling until the indicator changes from yellow to orange/red and stays; record the final reading and work out the volume of acid used; repeat with one tablet of each other brand (same mass or same number of tablets, same indicator amount); repeat each to get concordant results; brand needing the largest volume of acid neutralises the most.

practice.stem: A metal higher in the reactivity series than copper displaces copper from aqueous copper(II) sulfate, and the reaction releases heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to put three metals, magnesium, zinc and iron, in order of reactivity using the temperature change when each metal powder is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Say how you will use your results.
parts.answer: Fair temperature-change comparison with displacement.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: measure a fixed volume (e.g. 25 cm³) of copper(II) sulfate solution into a polystyrene cup; record the starting temperature with a thermometer; add a fixed mass (e.g. 1.0 g, an excess) of one metal powder; stir and record the highest temperature reached; repeat with each metal using fresh solution of the same concentration and same mass of powder; calculate the temperature rise; larger temperature rise = more reactive metal; repeat for reliable averages.

practice.stem:
A student adds a piece of magnesium ribbon to excess dilute sulfuric acid and collects the hydrogen in a gas syringe.
Time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180
Volume of gas / cm³: 0, 46, 66, 75, 79, 80, 80

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the rate of reaction changes during the experiment.
parts.answer: The rate is fastest at the start and decreases over time; it becomes zero by 150 s when the reaction stops.
parts.working: B1 fast then slower; B1 stops / zero by 150 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of reaction in the first 30 s, in cm³/s. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.5 cm³/s

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the total volume of hydrogen produced.
parts.answer: 80 cm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the reaction stops.
parts.answer: One of the reactants (the magnesium) has all been used up.
parts.working: B1 accept the limiting reactant is used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Different masses of magnesium are reacted with excess dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature and pressure. 1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³.
Mass of Mg / g: 0.024, 0.048, 0.072, 0.096
Volume of H₂ / cm³: 24, 48, 60, 96
Which mass gave an anomalous result?
A 0.024 g
B 0.048 g
C 0.072 g
D 0.096 g
parts.working: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂; each 0.024 g (0.001 mol) gives 24 cm³, so 0.072 g should give 72 cm³, not 60 cm³. The other results fit the 1 g : 1000 cm³ pattern.

practice.stem:
25.0 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid is placed in a polystyrene cup. Aqueous sodium hydroxide of concentration 1.00 mol/dm³ is added from a burette in portions, and the highest temperature is recorded after each addition.
Volume of NaOH / cm³: 0.0, 4.0, 8.0, 12.0, 16.0, 24.0, 28.0, 32.0, 36.0
Temperature / °C: 21.5, 24.0, 26.5, 27.6, 31.4, 33.0, 32.4, 31.8, 31.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which temperature reading is anomalous?
parts.answer: The reading at 12.0 cm³ (27.6 °C).
parts.working: B1 it lies below the straight line through the other early points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the two straight lines of best fit are drawn, the first line has the equation T = 21.5 + 0.62V and the second line has the equation T = 36.6 − 0.15V, where V is the volume of NaOH added in cm³. Calculate the volume of sodium hydroxide at which the lines meet. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 19.6 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid in mol/dm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.784 mol/dm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the temperature falls after the point where the two lines meet.
parts.answer: Neutralisation is complete; the cooler alkali added no longer reacts and heat is lost to the surroundings.

practice.stem:
A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid using methyl orange.
Titration 1: initial burette reading 3.40 cm³, final 28.35 cm³
Titration 2: initial 1.90 cm³, final 26.30 cm³
Titration 3: initial 0.10 cm³, final 24.55 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of acid used in each titration.
parts.answer: Titration 1: 24.95 cm³; titration 2: 24.40 cm³; titration 3: 24.45 cm³
parts.working: B1 for two correct; B1 for all three, to 2 d.p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which titrations are concordant and calculate the mean titre.
parts.answer: Titrations 2 and 3; mean = 24.43 cm³
parts.working: B1 2 and 3 (within 0.10 cm³); B1 mean 24.43 (accept 24.43 or 24.42).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why titration 1 gave a larger volume.
parts.answer: It was the rough (trial) titration and the end-point was overshot.

practice.stem:
The solubility of a salt Z in water was measured at different temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70
Solubility / g per 100 g water: 21, 32, 46, 64, 85, 110, 138

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to estimate the solubility of Z at 45 °C.
parts.answer: About 74 g per 100 g water (accept 72–76 from a smooth curve).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A saturated solution of Z in 50 g of water is cooled from 70 °C to 20 °C. Calculate the mass of Z that crystallises.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the trend shown by the data.
parts.answer: Solubility increases with temperature, and increases more steeply at higher temperatures.
parts.working: B1 both points for the mark: increases, and by larger amounts at high T.

practice.stem:
A student electrolyses aqueous copper(II) sulfate with a constant current and weighs the cathode at intervals.
Time / min: 5, 10, 15, 20, 30
Mass of copper deposited / g: 0.06, 0.12, 0.17, 0.24, 0.36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and suggest what its value should have been.
parts.answer: 15 min (0.17 g); should be 0.18 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the relationship between mass of copper deposited and time.
parts.answer: Mass is directly proportional to time.
parts.working: B1 accept straight line through the origin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the mass of copper deposited after 25 minutes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the 15-minute result was lower than expected.
parts.answer: Some copper fell off the cathode / cathode not dried properly before weighing / was weighed wet the other times / current changed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student needs exactly 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide to put into a conical flask for a titration. Which apparatus should be used?
A beaker
B measuring cylinder
C volumetric pipette
D gas syringe
parts.answer: C volumetric pipette
parts.working: A volumetric pipette delivers a fixed volume accurately (25.0 cm³). A measuring cylinder is less accurate; a beaker only gives a rough volume; a gas syringe is for gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The burette reading is 12.60 cm³ before the titration and 36.15 cm³ after. Calculate the volume added.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A stop-watch shows 1:23 (minutes:seconds). Give this time in seconds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the units used for the volume of a gas collected in a gas syringe.
parts.answer: cm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the piece of apparatus used to measure the mass of a solid.
parts.answer: (Electronic / top-pan) balance

practice.stem: A thermometer has 1 °C divisions. At the start the liquid level is halfway between the 19 °C and 20 °C marks. At the end it is level with the 27 °C mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Record the starting and final temperatures to the nearest 0.5 °C.
parts.answer: Start 19.5 °C; final 27.0 °C
parts.working: B1 each; both must show one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why recording the final temperature as '27' is not acceptable.
parts.answer: Readings must be recorded to the same resolution/precision as the thermometer allows, i.e. 27.0 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which apparatus is best for measuring the volume of carbon dioxide given off every 20 seconds during a reaction?
A a burette
B a gas syringe
C a volumetric pipette
D a balance
parts.answer: B a gas syringe
parts.working: A gas syringe collects the gas and shows its volume directly at any time. A burette and pipette measure liquid volumes; a balance can follow the mass lost, not the volume.

practice.stem: A student in Islamabad titrates 25.0 cm³ of aqueous potassium hydroxide with dilute nitric acid from a burette.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the burette is rinsed with the acid, not water, before it is filled.
parts.answer: Water would dilute the acid and change its concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the conical flask is placed on a white tile.
parts.answer: To see the colour change of the indicator more clearly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Thymolphthalein is used as the indicator. State the colour change at the end-point when acid is added to the alkali.
parts.answer: Blue to colourless.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the acid is added drop by drop near the end-point and the flask swirled.
parts.answer: So the end-point is not overshot; swirling mixes the reactants so the indicator change is permanent/accurate.

practice.stem: Three students carry out the same titration of 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide with dilute hydrochloric acid, but each makes a different change to the method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Student 1 left an air bubble in the burette tip, which came out during the titration. State and explain the effect on the measured titre.
parts.answer: The titre is too large: the bubble's volume is counted as acid added though no acid was delivered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Student 2 rinsed the pipette with water and did not dry it before measuring the alkali. State and explain the effect on the measured titre.
parts.answer: The titre is too small: the alkali is diluted, so the 25.0 cm³ contains fewer moles of alkali and needs less acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Student 3 added water to the conical flask during the titration to wash the sides. State the effect on the titre.
parts.answer: No effect: the number of moles of alkali in the flask is unchanged.

practice.stem: Separating mixtures is an important skill in a chemistry laboratory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how pure, dry crystals of salt can be obtained from a mixture of sand and salt.
parts.answer: Add water and stir to dissolve the salt; filter to remove sand (residue); heat the filtrate to evaporate some water until crystals start to form / to the point of crystallisation; leave to cool and crystallise, then filter and dry the crystals (on filter paper).
parts.working: 1 mark each for dissolve, filter, evaporate to crystallisation point, cool/dry crystals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the method used to separate ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) from water.
parts.answer: Fractional distillation

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this method works.
parts.answer: Ethanol has a lower boiling point so it evaporates first and is condensed and collected first.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A pure substance melts at 136 °C. A student's sample of the same substance melts over the range 128 °C to 133 °C. Which conclusion is correct?
A The sample is pure, because it melts below 136 °C.
B The sample is impure, because it melts over a range below 136 °C.
C The sample is impure, because impurities raise the melting point.
D The sample is a different substance, because pure substances have no melting point.
parts.answer: B The sample is impure, because it melts over a range below 136 °C.
parts.working: Impurities lower the melting point and make the substance melt over a range of temperatures. C is wrong because impurities lower, not raise, the melting point.

practice.stem: A food colouring used in mithai (sweets) is tested by paper chromatography. The solvent front moves 8.0 cm from the starting line. The colouring gives two spots, at 2.4 cm and 5.6 cm from the starting line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Rf values of the two spots.
parts.working: B1 each: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the starting line is drawn in pencil, not ink.
parts.answer: Pencil (graphite) does not dissolve in the solvent / move up the paper; ink would separate and interfere.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the starting line must be above the level of the solvent.
parts.answer: Otherwise the dyes dissolve into the solvent in the beaker instead of moving up the paper.

parts.label: d
parts.text: How many dyes are in the food colouring?
parts.answer: Two

practice.stem:
A sample containing one amino acid is analysed by chromatography. The solvent front travels 12.5 cm and the spot travels 4.0 cm.
Rf values of amino acids in this solvent: glycine 0.26; alanine 0.32; valine 0.51; leucine 0.70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Amino acids are colourless. State what must be done to the chromatogram so that the spots can be seen.
parts.answer: Spray it with a locating agent (and dry/heat).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value of the spot. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the table to identify the amino acid.
parts.answer: Alanine

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the Rf values in the table are only useful if the same solvent is used.
parts.answer: Rf depends on the solvent: how soluble the substance is in it and how strongly it is attracted to the paper change with the solvent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of polymerisation used to make poly(ethene) from ethene.
parts.answer: addition polymerisation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of poly(ethene) as a structural formula.
parts.answer: –CH₂–CH₂–
parts.working: Accept a written description: two carbon atoms joined by a single bond, each with two H atoms, with continuation bonds at both ends.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two problems caused by the disposal of poly(ethene) shopping bags.
parts.answer: Any two of: non-biodegradable, so they stay in landfill for a long time; litter and harm to animals (e.g. in rivers and seas); burning releases toxic gases / greenhouse gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why plastic bottles found on a beach in Karachi can stay there for hundreds of years.
parts.answer: Plastics are non-biodegradable (not broken down by microorganisms).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of burning waste plastics.
parts.answer: It releases toxic gases / carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing the amount of plastic waste.
parts.answer: Recycling (e.g. PET bottles) / reusing / using less plastic packaging.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Poly(chloroethene) is used to make water pipes. What is its monomer?
A CH₃CH₂Cl
B CH₂=CHCl
C CH₂Cl–CH₂Cl
D CCl₂=CCl₂
parts.answer: B CH₂=CHCl
parts.working: An addition polymer is made from an alkene; chloroethene is CH₂=CHCl. A has no C=C double bond, so it cannot undergo addition polymerisation.

practice.stem: Poly(propene) is used to make ropes for fishing boats in Gwadar. It is made from propene, CH₃CH=CH₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the repeat unit of poly(propene).
parts.answer: –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative formula mass of one repeat unit. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1]

parts.label: c
parts.text: A molecule of poly(propene) has a relative molecular mass of 84 000. Calculate the number of repeat units in the molecule.

practice.stem: Lentils (daal) are a good source of protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the monomers from which proteins are made.
parts.answer: amino acids

parts.label: b
parts.text: Proteins are natural polyamides. Name the type of polymerisation that forms them.
parts.answer: condensation polymerisation

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the name of the small molecule released each time two monomers join.
parts.answer: water

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the name of the synthetic polymer that has the same linkage as proteins.
parts.answer: nylon

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nylon is made from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine. Name the type of polymerisation and the small molecule formed.
parts.answer: condensation polymerisation; water

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the linkage in nylon and give its structure.
parts.answer: amide linkage; –CONH– (–CO–NH–)

parts.label: c
parts.text: PET is made from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol. Name the type of linkage in PET.
parts.answer: ester linkage (–COO–)

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two differences between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.
parts.answer: Addition: only one product (the polymer) and monomers have C=C bonds; condensation: a small molecule (e.g. water) is also formed and monomers have two functional groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
PET is used to make drinks bottles. Which linkage joins the monomer units in PET?
A –CONH–
B –COO–
C –C=C–
D –O–H
parts.answer: B –COO–
parts.working: PET is a polyester; its linkage is the ester group –COO–. A is the amide linkage found in nylon and proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound is an alkane?
A C₅H₁₀
B C₅H₁₂
C C₅H₈
D C₅H₁₁OH
parts.answer: B C₅H₁₂
parts.working: Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: n = 5 gives C₅H₁₂. A fits CₙH₂ₙ, the alkenes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three characteristics of a homologous series.
parts.answer: Any three of: same general formula; same functional group; similar chemical properties; trend in physical properties; each member differs from the next by CH₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the name of the homologous series with the functional group –OH.
parts.answer: alcohols

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by structural isomers.
parts.answer: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
parts.working: B1 same molecular formula; B1 different structural formula.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formulae of the two structural isomers with molecular formula C₄H₁₀.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the unbranched isomer.
parts.answer: butane

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the functional group present in each compound: (i) propanoic acid, (ii) but-1-ene, (iii) propan-1-ol.
parts.answer: (i) carboxylic acid, –COOH; (ii) C=C double bond (alkene); (iii) hydroxyl, –OH (alcohol)

parts.label: b
parts.text: But-1-ene and but-2-ene have the formula C₄H₈. Give the structural formula of each and state how they are related.
parts.answer: but-1-ene CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃; but-2-ene CH₃CH=CHCH₃; they are structural isomers

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the compounds: (i) CH₃CH₂OH, (ii) CH₃COOH, (iii) CH₃CH=CH₂, (iv) CH₃COOCH₃.
parts.answer: (i) ethanol; (ii) ethanoic acid; (iii) propene; (iv) methyl ethanoate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of the alkene with six carbon atoms and calculate its relative molecular mass. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1]
parts.answer: C₆H₁₂; 84

practice.stem: Vinegar contains ethanoic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when magnesium ribbon is added to aqueous ethanoic acid, and name the products.
parts.answer: Fizzing / bubbles and the magnesium dissolves (slowly); magnesium ethanoate and hydrogen.
parts.working: B1 observation; B1 magnesium ethanoate; B1 hydrogen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the salt formed when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate.
parts.answer: sodium ethanoate

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: It is only partially dissociated (ionised) in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which ester is formed when ethanol reacts with propanoic acid?
A propyl ethanoate
B ethyl propanoate
C ethyl ethanoate
D propyl propanoate
parts.answer: B ethyl propanoate
parts.working: The alcohol gives the first part of the name (ethyl) and the acid gives the second part (propanoate). A reverses the two parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the conditions needed to make an ester from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid.
parts.answer: Heat (warm); concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the word equation for the reaction between methanol and ethanoic acid.
parts.answer: methanol + ethanoic acid ⇌ methyl ethanoate + water
parts.working: B1 methyl ethanoate; B1 water. Accept → arrow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one use of esters.
parts.answer: flavourings / perfumes / solvents

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanoic acid can be made by heating ethanol with acidified potassium manganate(VII). State the colour change and the type of reaction.
parts.answer: Purple to colourless; oxidation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name another method of making ethanoic acid from ethanol.
parts.answer: Bacterial oxidation / fermentation by bacteria (in air), as in making vinegar.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ethanoic acid that can be made from 9.2 g of ethanol. [Mr: ethanol = 46, ethanoic acid = 60]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propyl ethanoate smells of pears. Name the alcohol and the carboxylic acid used to make it.
parts.answer: propan-1-ol (propanol); ethanoic acid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formula of propyl ethanoate.
parts.answer: CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the molecular formula of propyl ethanoate and calculate its relative molecular mass. [Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]
parts.answer: C₅H₁₀O₂; 102

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What are the products of the complete combustion of ethanol?
A carbon monoxide and water
B carbon dioxide and hydrogen
C carbon dioxide and water
D carbon and water
parts.answer: C carbon dioxide and water
parts.working: Complete combustion in plenty of oxygen gives CO₂ and H₂O. A and D are products of incomplete combustion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two uses of ethanol.
parts.answer: solvent; fuel
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept: in hand sanitisers (as a solvent / antiseptic).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.
parts.answer: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O

practice.stem: Pakistan makes ethanol from sugar-cane molasses. Ethanol can also be made from ethene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the conditions for making ethanol by fermentation.
parts.answer: Yeast; about 25–35 °C; absence of oxygen (anaerobic); aqueous sugar (glucose).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the conditions for making ethanol from ethene and steam.
parts.answer: about 300 °C; about 6000 kPa (60 atm); phosphoric acid catalyst

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage of fermentation and one advantage of the hydration of ethene.
parts.answer: Fermentation: uses a renewable raw material (sugar cane) / low temperature; hydration: faster / continuous / produces pure ethanol.

practice.stem: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol formed from 45 g of glucose. [Mr: glucose = 180, ethanol = 46]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed at room temperature and pressure, in dm³. [1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
parts.answer: 12.0 dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the fermentation stops when the ethanol concentration reaches about 15 %.
parts.answer: The yeast is killed (denatured) by the high ethanol concentration.

practice.stem: Two unlabelled bottles contain hexane and hexene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a chemical test to show which liquid is hexene.
parts.answer: Add bromine water; hexene turns it from orange to colourless, hexane leaves it orange.
parts.working: B1 bromine water; B1 orange to colourless with hexene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why hexene is described as unsaturated.
parts.answer: It contains a C=C double bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the product when ethene reacts with hydrogen, and state the catalyst.
parts.answer: ethane; nickel

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product when ethene reacts with steam.
parts.answer: ethanol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the product when ethene reacts with bromine.
parts.answer: 1,2-dibromoethane

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the type of reaction in (a), (b) and (c).
parts.answer: addition

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Propene reacts with bromine. What is the molecular formula of the product?
A C₃H₅Br
B C₃H₆Br₂
C C₃H₇Br
D C₃H₈Br₂
parts.answer: B C₃H₆Br₂
parts.working: Addition across the C=C bond adds both bromine atoms and keeps all six H atoms: C₃H₆ + Br₂ → C₃H₆Br₂. A would be a substitution product.

practice.stem: LPG cylinders used for cooking in many Pakistani homes contain propane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane.
parts.answer: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the toxic gas produced if the supply of air to the cooker is limited.
parts.answer: carbon monoxide

parts.label: c
parts.text: Apart from combustion, alkanes are generally unreactive. Explain why, in terms of bonding.
parts.answer: They contain only single C–C and C–H bonds (saturated).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of reaction between methane and chlorine.
parts.answer: substitution (photochemical)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the condition needed.
parts.answer: ultraviolet (UV) light

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction that forms chloromethane.
parts.answer: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain the role of the UV light.
parts.answer: It provides the energy to break the Cl–Cl bond (start the reaction).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
50 cm³ of butane, C₄H₁₀, is burned completely in oxygen. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. What volume of oxygen is needed?
A 200 cm³
B 250 cm³
C 325 cm³
D 400 cm³
parts.answer: C 325 cm³
parts.working: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O, so 1 volume of butane needs 6.5 volumes of O₂: 50 × 6.5 = 325 cm³. A is the volume of CO₂ formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process used to separate petroleum into fractions.
parts.answer: fractional distillation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one use of each fraction: (i) refinery gas, (ii) kerosene, (iii) bitumen, (iv) naphtha.
parts.answer: (i) heating and cooking; (ii) jet fuel; (iii) surfacing roads (and roofs); (iv) feedstock for making chemicals

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how chain length changes from the top to the bottom of the fractionating column.
parts.answer: Chain length increases (molecules get larger) towards the bottom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two conditions used to crack long-chain alkanes.
parts.answer: high temperature; catalyst

parts.label: b
parts.text: Complete the equation: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + ______
parts.answer: C₂H₄

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why cracking is carried out.
parts.answer: To meet the demand for shorter-chain alkanes such as petrol; to produce alkenes for making polymers (and hydrogen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hexadecane, C₁₆H₃₄, is cracked to form octane, C₈H₁₈, two molecules of propene and one molecule of compound Z. Deduce the molecular formula of Z.
parts.answer: C₂H₄

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name compound Z and state the homologous series to which it belongs.
parts.answer: ethene; alkenes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the supply of long-chain fractions from fractional distillation is greater than the demand for them.
parts.answer: Petroleum naturally contains a large proportion of long-chain hydrocarbons, but they have few uses (e.g. fuel oil, bitumen), so less is needed than is produced.
parts.working: Accept: more long chains in crude oil than are needed / demand is mainly for short chains such as petrol.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated until it turns white. When the white solid has cooled, a few drops of water are added. What is observed and why?
A The solid stays white because the reaction cannot be reversed.
B The solid turns blue and gets warm because the reaction is reversible.
C The solid turns blue and gets cold because water is absorbed.
D The solid dissolves to form a colourless solution.
parts.answer: B The solid turns blue and gets warm because the reaction is reversible.
parts.working: CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O is reversible; the forward reaction is endothermic so the reverse (adding water) is exothermic and the solid gets warm. C has the energy change the wrong way round.

practice.stem: A reversible reaction is allowed to reach equilibrium in a closed system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a closed system.
parts.answer: A system in which no substances can enter or leave.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the equilibrium is described as dynamic.
parts.answer: The forward and reverse reactions are still happening, at the same rate.
parts.working: B1 both reactions continue; B1 at equal rates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by the symbol ⇌.
parts.answer: The reaction is reversible.

practice.stem:
Dinitrogen tetroxide (colourless) and nitrogen dioxide (brown) form an equilibrium in a sealed tube:
N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)   the forward reaction is endothermic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sealed tube is placed in hot water. State and explain what happens to the colour of the gas mixture.
parts.answer: It becomes darker brown, because the forward reaction is endothermic so the equilibrium shifts to the right, producing more NO₂.
parts.working: B1 darker brown; B1 equilibrium moves in endothermic direction / to the right.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas mixture is compressed in a gas syringe at constant temperature. State and explain how the position of equilibrium changes.
parts.answer: It moves to the left, because there are fewer moles of gas on the left (1 mol compared with 2 mol), so this reduces the pressure.
parts.working: B1 shifts left (towards N₂O₄); B1 fewer gas molecules on left.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Methanol is made by the reaction CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. Which conditions give the highest equilibrium yield of methanol?
A high temperature and high pressure
B high temperature and low pressure
C low temperature and high pressure
D low temperature and low pressure
parts.answer: C low temperature and high pressure
parts.working: Low temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction; high pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (3 → 1). A would give a faster rate, but a lower yield.

practice.stem:
In aqueous solution, yellow chromate(VI) ions and orange dichromate(VI) ions form an equilibrium:
2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
  yellow                          orange

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dilute sulfuric acid is added to the yellow solution. State and explain the colour change.
parts.answer: It turns orange, because adding H⁺ ions moves the equilibrium to the right, forming more Cr₂O₇²⁻.
parts.working: B1 orange; B1 more H⁺ moves equilibrium right.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is then added to the orange solution. Suggest what is seen. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: It turns yellow again, because OH⁻ ions react with (remove) H⁺ ions, so the equilibrium moves to the left.
parts.working: B1 yellow; B1 H⁺ removed so equilibrium shifts left.

practice.stem:
Hydrogen and iodine react in a closed container:
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of a system at dynamic equilibrium.
parts.answer: The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction; the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept: closed system needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the position of equilibrium.
parts.answer: No effect, because there are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side (2 and 2).
parts.working: B1 no change; B1 same number of gas moles on both sides.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect of increasing the pressure on the rate at which equilibrium is reached. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The rate increases, because the gas particles are closer together, so there are more collisions per unit time.
parts.working: B1 faster; B1 higher collision frequency.

practice.stem:
A gas XY₃ is made by the reaction X₂(g) + 3Y₂(g) ⇌ 2XY₃(g). The percentage of XY₃ at equilibrium is:
200 °C: 50 % at 10 000 kPa; 70 % at 30 000 kPa
400 °C: 15 % at 10 000 kPa; 35 % at 30 000 kPa
600 °C: 3 % at 10 000 kPa; 9 % at 30 000 kPa

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Exothermic: the yield of XY₃ decreases as temperature increases, so the equilibrium shifts left (endothermic direction) when heated.
parts.working: B1 exothermic; B1 yield falls with increasing temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the yield.
parts.answer: Yield increases, because the equilibrium shifts to the right, the side with fewer moles of gas (2 compared with 4).
parts.working: B1 yield increases (data); B1 fewer gas moles on right.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the manufacturer chooses 400 °C rather than 200 °C, even though the yield is lower.
parts.answer: At 200 °C the rate is too slow; 400 °C gives an acceptable yield at a faster rate (compromise).
parts.working: B1 rate too slow at low temperature; B1 compromise between rate and yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the effect of adding a catalyst on the position of equilibrium.
parts.answer: No effect / the position does not change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a catalyst is still used in many industrial equilibrium reactions.
parts.answer: It increases the rates of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached more quickly, saving time and energy costs.
parts.working: B1 increases both rates equally; B1 equilibrium reached faster / lower temperature can be used.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
parts.answer: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react.
parts.working: B1 lower activation energy / alternative route; B1 more particles have energy ≥ Ea / more successful collisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Magnesium ribbon reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which change increases the rate of the reaction?
A using a larger volume of the same acid
B increasing the temperature of the acid
C using a wider beaker
D adding water to the acid
parts.answer: B increasing the temperature of the acid
parts.working: A higher temperature gives particles more energy, so more frequent and more successful collisions. A does not change concentration so the rate is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a catalyst.
parts.answer: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged (chemically and in mass) at the end.
parts.working: B1 increases rate; B1 unchanged at the end.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly into water and oxygen. Name a catalyst for this reaction.
parts.answer: manganese(IV) oxide (MnO₂) / catalase

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test for the oxygen given off.
parts.answer: It relights a glowing splint.

practice.stem: A student in Peshawar reacts marble chips (calcium carbonate) with excess dilute hydrochloric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student repeats the experiment using the same mass of powdered marble. Explain, in terms of particles, why the reaction is faster.
parts.answer: Powder has a larger surface area, so more particles of calcium carbonate are exposed and the frequency of collisions with acid particles increases.
parts.working: B1 larger surface area; B1 more collisions per unit time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student then uses hydrochloric acid of half the concentration with the original marble chips. Explain the effect on the rate.
parts.answer: The rate decreases, because there are fewer acid particles per unit volume, so collisions are less frequent.
parts.working: B1 slower; B1 fewer particles per unit volume, lower collision frequency.

practice.stem:
Zinc granules react with dilute hydrochloric acid. The hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe.
time / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 210, 240
volume / cm³: 0, 24, 42, 55, 63, 67, 69, 70, 70

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the total volume of gas produced.
parts.answer: 70 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of reaction in the first 60 s, in cm³/s.
parts.answer: 0.7 cm³/s

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate of reaction decreases as the reaction goes on.
parts.answer: Reactants are used up (the concentration of the acid decreases), so there are fewer collisions per unit time.
parts.working: B1 reactant(s) used up / concentration of acid falls; B1 fewer collisions per second.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest the time at which the reaction stopped.
parts.answer: Between 180 s and 210 s
parts.working: First time the volume reaches 70 cm³ is 210 s; accept any time from 180 s to 210 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A flask containing marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid is placed on a balance and its mass is recorded every minute. The acid is in excess. Which change would make the mass fall faster but give the same total loss in mass?
A using the same mass of powdered marble
B using a smaller mass of marble chips
C using a larger volume of the same acid
D using a cotton wool plug in the flask
parts.answer: A using the same mass of powdered marble
parts.working: Powder increases surface area, so the rate rises, and the same mass of marble gives the same mass of CO₂. B would give a smaller total loss.

practice.stem:
Calcium carbonate is added to dilute nitric acid in a conical flask on a balance.
mass of flask and contents at start = 152.40 g
mass after 5 minutes = 151.52 g (the reaction had stopped)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of reaction over the 5 minutes, in g/min.
parts.answer: 0.176 g/min

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of carbon dioxide lost. [Mr of CO₂ = 44]

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why a loose cotton wool plug is placed in the neck of the flask.
parts.answer: To let the gas escape but stop acid spray / liquid being lost (which would give extra mass loss).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of collisions and activation energy, why increasing the temperature increases the rate of a reaction.
parts.answer: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide more often; a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so more collisions are successful.
parts.working: B1 more kinetic energy / faster particles; B1 more frequent collisions; B1 more particles with energy ≥ activation energy (more successful collisions).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why milk kept in a refrigerator goes sour more slowly than milk left out on a hot day in Multan.
parts.answer: Lower temperature slows the reactions (of bacteria / enzymes) that sour the milk.

practice.stem:
Sodium thiosulfate solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form a cloudy mixture. A flask is placed on a cross drawn on paper and the time for the cross to disappear is measured. 10 cm³ of acid is used each time.
experiment 1: 50 cm³ thiosulfate, 0 cm³ water, 20 s
experiment 2: 40 cm³ thiosulfate, 10 cm³ water, 25 s
experiment 3: 30 cm³ thiosulfate, 20 cm³ water, 34 s
experiment 4: 20 cm³ thiosulfate, 30 cm³ water, 62 s
experiment 5: 10 cm³ thiosulfate, 40 cm³ water, 101 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of 1/time for experiment 1. Give the unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result. Explain your choice.
parts.answer: Experiment 4 (20 cm³), 62 s; the pattern suggests about 50 s, as halving the concentration from experiment 2 should double the time.
parts.working: B1 experiment 4; B1 reason based on trend (expected ~50 s).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why water was added so that the total volume was always 50 cm³.
parts.answer: So that the volume of thiosulfate is proportional to its concentration, and the depth of liquid over the cross is the same (fair test).
parts.working: B1 concentration proportional to volume used; B1 same depth / fair test.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the solid that makes the mixture cloudy.
parts.answer: sulfur

practice.stem: Ammonia is manufactured by the Haber process at fertiliser plants in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced symbol equation for the Haber process, including the reversible sign.
parts.answer: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sources of the nitrogen and of the hydrogen.
parts.answer: Nitrogen from the air; hydrogen from methane (natural gas) reacting with steam.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the temperature, pressure and catalyst used.
parts.answer: about 450 °C; about 20 000 kPa (200 atm); iron catalyst

practice.stem: The Contact process is used to make sulfuric acid. In the converter: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g); the forward reaction is exothermic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the source of the oxygen used in the converter.
parts.answer: air

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the catalyst used in the converter.
parts.answer: vanadium(V) oxide (V₂O₅)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the equilibrium yield of sulfur trioxide.
parts.answer: The yield decreases, because the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts to the left (the endothermic direction).
parts.working: B1 yield decreases; B1 forward reaction exothermic / equilibrium moves in endothermic direction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the final product of the Contact process and give its formula.
parts.answer: sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which the sulfur dioxide for the Contact process is obtained.
parts.answer: Burning sulfur in air; roasting sulfide ores (e.g. zinc sulfide, iron pyrites) in air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction in the converter, and state the conditions used.
parts.answer: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃; about 450 °C, about 200 kPa (2 atm), vanadium(V) oxide catalyst
parts.working: B1 equation with ⇌; B1 temperature and pressure; B1 V₂O₅.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Higher pressure would increase the yield, but only about 200 kPa is used. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The yield is already high at low pressure, so the extra cost of high-pressure equipment is not worth it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which set of conditions is used in the Haber process?
A 200 °C, 200 kPa, vanadium(V) oxide
B 450 °C, 200 kPa, iron
C 450 °C, 20 000 kPa, iron
D 1000 °C, 20 000 kPa, nickel
parts.answer: C 450 °C, 20 000 kPa, iron
parts.working: The Haber process uses about 450 °C, 20 000 kPa and an iron catalyst. B uses the Contact process pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The forward reaction in the Haber process is exothermic. Explain why a temperature of about 450 °C is used rather than a lower temperature.
parts.answer: A lower temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield, but the rate would be too slow; 450 °C is a compromise giving a reasonable yield at an acceptable rate.
parts.working: B1 lower T gives higher yield; B1 but rate too slow; B1 compromise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a pressure higher than 20 000 kPa is not used.
parts.answer: Higher pressure would increase yield but equipment would be very expensive to build and run, and it is more dangerous.
parts.working: B1 cost of equipment / energy; B1 safety.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Only about 15 % of the gases react in each pass through the reactor. Suggest what happens to the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen.
parts.answer: They are recycled (passed back over the catalyst).

practice.stem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of ammonia, in tonnes, that could be made from 1.40 tonnes of nitrogen. [Ar: N = 14, H = 1]
parts.answer: 1.70 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one pass through the reactor only 15 % of this mass is formed. Calculate the mass of ammonia formed in one pass.
parts.answer: 0.255 tonnes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define oxidation in terms of (i) oxygen and (ii) electrons.
parts.answer: (i) gain of oxygen; (ii) loss of electrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: For the reaction CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, name the substance that is reduced and the substance that is oxidised.
parts.answer: CuO (copper(II) oxide) is reduced; H₂ (hydrogen) is oxidised.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the oxidation number of manganese in potassium manganate(VII), KMnO₄?
A +2
B +4
C +6
D +7
parts.working: K is +1 and four O are 4 × (−2) = −8, so Mn = +7, as shown by (VII) in the name. C (+6) is the oxidation number in a manganate(VI); A and B are other common oxidation numbers of manganese (Mn²⁺, MnO₂).

practice.stem:
Zinc powder is added to blue copper(II) sulfate solution. The blue colour fades and a pink-brown solid forms.
Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the change to zinc.
parts.answer: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the change to copper(II) ions.
parts.answer: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Oxidising agent: Cu²⁺ (it gains electrons / is reduced); reducing agent: Zn (it loses electrons / is oxidised).
parts.working: B1 Cu²⁺ oxidising agent; B1 Zn reducing agent; B1 explanation in terms of electron transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solution P is added to acidified potassium manganate(VII). The purple colour disappears. State what this shows about P.
parts.answer: P is a reducing agent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solution Q is added to aqueous potassium iodide. The colourless solution turns brown. State what this shows about Q, and name the substance causing the brown colour.
parts.answer: Q is an oxidising agent; iodine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student adds an oxidising agent to acidified potassium manganate(VII). State what the student sees. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: No change / the solution stays purple, because acidified potassium manganate(VII) is itself an oxidising agent and is only decolourised by a reducing agent.
parts.working: B1 stays purple / no colour change; B1 KMnO₄ is an oxidising agent, it needs a reducing agent to react.

practice.stem: Household bleach contains sodium chlorate(I), NaClO.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of chlorine in: (i) Cl₂, (ii) NaCl, (iii) NaClO, (iv) the chlorate ion ClO₃⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chlorine reacts with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. Use oxidation numbers to explain why this is a redox reaction.
parts.answer: Chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (reduced, in NaCl) and from 0 to +1 (oxidised, in NaClO); reduction and oxidation both occur.

practice.stem:
In the blast furnace, iron(III) oxide is reduced:
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of iron in Fe₂O₃ and in Fe.
parts.answer: +3 in Fe₂O₃; 0 in Fe

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of carbon in CO and in CO₂.
parts.answer: +2 in CO; +4 in CO₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to identify the reducing agent. State how many electrons are gained by each iron ion.
parts.answer: CO is the reducing agent (C is oxidised from +2 to +4); 3 electrons per iron ion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a chemical change?
A ice melting in a glass of water
B sugar dissolving in tea
C an iron gate rusting
D water boiling in a kettle
parts.answer: C an iron gate rusting
parts.working: Rusting forms a new substance (hydrated iron(III) oxide). The others are physical changes that only change the state or mix substances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between a physical change and a chemical change.
parts.answer: A chemical change forms a new substance, a physical change does not; physical changes are usually easily reversed, chemical changes usually are not.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept: chemical change usually has a large energy change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify each of the following as a physical or chemical change: (i) burning natural gas in a cooking stove, (ii) iodine subliming, (iii) frying an egg, (iv) dissolving salt in water.
parts.answer: (i) chemical; (ii) physical; (iii) chemical; (iv) physical
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct, 1 mark for three correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An ion of iron is written as ⁵⁶₂₆Fe³⁺. How many protons, neutrons and electrons does this ion contain?
A 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 23 electrons
B 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 29 electrons
C 26 protons, 56 neutrons, 23 electrons
D 30 protons, 26 neutrons, 23 electrons
parts.answer: A 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 23 electrons
parts.working: Proton number 26; neutrons = 56 − 26 = 30; a 3+ ion has lost 3 electrons, so 26 − 3 = 23. B adds 3 electrons instead of removing them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the following: an atom has a central ______ containing protons and ______, surrounded by ______ in shells.
parts.answer: nucleus; neutrons; electrons
parts.working: 2 marks for all three correct, 1 mark for two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of a magnesium atom (proton number 12).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Magnesium has three isotopes. State why all three isotopes react in the same way with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: They have the same number of outer-shell electrons / the same electronic configuration.
parts.working: Chemical properties depend on electrons, not neutrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the relative mass and relative charge of: (i) a proton, (ii) a neutron, (iii) an electron.
parts.answer: proton: mass 1, charge +1; neutron: mass 1, charge 0; electron: mass 1/1840 (negligible), charge −1
parts.working: 1 mark for each particle with both values correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which two of these particles are found in the nucleus.
parts.answer: protons and neutrons

practice.stem: Phosphorus is one of the three main nutrient elements in fertilisers used on wheat farms in Punjab. A phosphorus atom has 15 electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of a phosphorus atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to (a) to state the group and the period of phosphorus in the Periodic Table.
parts.answer: Group V; Period 3
parts.working: B1 group V (5 outer electrons); B1 period 3 (three shells).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of protons in the nucleus of a phosphorus atom.

practice.stem: Gallium is used in semiconductors for LED lights. A sample of gallium contains 60.1 % of gallium-69 and 39.9 % of gallium-71.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the term isotopes.
parts.answer: Atoms of the same element (same number of protons / same proton number) with different numbers of neutrons (different nucleon numbers).
parts.working: B1 same proton number / same element; B1 different number of neutrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of gallium. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in one atom of gallium-71 (proton number 31).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of atoms are isotopes of the same element? (Values given as nucleon number, proton number.)
A (40, 18) and (40, 20)
B (35, 17) and (37, 17)
C (14, 6) and (14, 7)
D (23, 11) and (24, 12)
parts.working: Isotopes have the same proton number but different nucleon numbers: 17 and 17 with 35 and 37. A has the same nucleon number but different proton numbers, so they are different elements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Particle X has 17 protons, 20 neutrons and 18 electrons. Write the symbol of X, showing its nucleon number and charge.
parts.answer: ³⁷Cl⁻
parts.working: B1 Cl with nucleon number 37; B1 charge 1− (one more electron than protons).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Particle Y has 12 protons, 12 neutrons and 10 electrons. Write the symbol of Y, showing its nucleon number and charge.
parts.answer: ²⁴Mg²⁺
parts.working: B1 Mg with nucleon number 24; B1 charge 2+.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of a sulfide ion, S²⁻ (proton number of sulfur 16).

practice.stem: Boron compounds are used in heat-resistant glass. Natural boron is a mixture of only two isotopes, boron-10 and boron-11. The relative atomic mass of boron is 10.81.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let the percentage of boron-10 be x. Write an expression for the relative atomic mass of boron in terms of x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of boron-10 atoms in natural boron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of neutrons in an atom of boron-11. The proton number of boron is 5.

practice.stem:
A mass spectrometer in a university laboratory in Islamabad gives these results for a sample of magnesium:
magnesium-24: 78.99 %
magnesium-25: 10.00 %
magnesium-26: 11.01 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of neutrons in one atom of magnesium-26. The proton number of magnesium is 12.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says that magnesium-26 must be more reactive than magnesium-24 because it is heavier. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Both isotopes have 12 electrons with the same arrangement (2 outer electrons), and reactivity depends on the electrons, not on the number of neutrons.
parts.working: B1 same electronic configuration / same number of outer electrons; B1 neutrons do not affect chemical reactions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Calcium forms Ca²⁺ ions and nitrogen forms N³⁻ ions. What is the formula of calcium nitride?
A CaN
B Ca₂N₃
C Ca₃N₂
D CaN₂
parts.answer: C Ca₃N₂
parts.working: Charges must balance: 3 × (+2) = +6 and 2 × (−3) = −6, so Ca₃N₂. B swaps the numbers the wrong way round.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configurations of a lithium atom and a fluorine atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formulae, with charges, of the two ions in lithium fluoride.
parts.answer: Li⁺ and F⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of bonding in lithium fluoride.
parts.answer: ionic

practice.stem: Magnesium oxide is used to line the inside of furnaces in steel works.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in terms of electrons, how a magnesium atom and an oxygen atom form magnesium oxide. Give the electronic configurations of both ions formed.
parts.answer: Magnesium atom loses its two outer electrons, oxygen atom gains two electrons; Mg²⁺ is 2,8 and O²⁻ is 2,8.
parts.working: B1 two electrons transferred from Mg to O; B1 Mg²⁺ 2,8; B1 O²⁻ 2,8.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why magnesium oxide has a very high melting point.
parts.answer: It has a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; a lot of energy is needed to overcome these forces.
parts.working: B1 strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; B1 lots of energy needed to overcome them / giant lattice.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which ions all have the same electronic configuration as a neon atom?
A Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Cl⁻
B Li⁺, F⁻, O²⁻
C Na⁺, Al³⁺, O²⁻
D K⁺, Ca²⁺, S²⁻
parts.answer: C Na⁺, Al³⁺, O²⁻
parts.working: Na⁺, Al³⁺ and O²⁻ each have 10 electrons (2,8). A includes Cl⁻ (2,8,8); D are all 2,8,8 like argon; Li⁺ in B is 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the formula of aluminium oxide, which contains Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions.
parts.answer: Al₂O₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of electrons transferred when the ions in one formula unit of aluminium oxide are formed from atoms.
parts.working: M1 each Al loses 3 electrons and there are 2 Al; A1 6 (= 3 O atoms × 2 electrons).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formula of potassium sulfide.
parts.answer: K₂S

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does.
parts.answer: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move; when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 ions fixed in solid; B1 ions mobile when molten. (Reject 'electrons move'.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The melting point of sodium chloride is 801 °C and the melting point of magnesium oxide is 2852 °C. Suggest why the melting point of magnesium oxide is much higher.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have larger charges than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the electrostatic attraction between the ions is stronger and needs more energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 ions have charges 2+ / 2− compared with 1+ / 1−; B1 stronger attraction, more energy needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the structure of solid sodium chloride.
parts.answer: A giant lattice of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a regular repeating arrangement.
parts.working: B1 giant lattice; B1 regular alternating positive and negative ions.

practice.stem: Ammonia is used to make urea fertiliser at plants near Daharki.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an ammonia molecule, NH₃, state the number of bonding pairs of electrons and the number of non-bonding (lone) pairs on the nitrogen atom.
parts.answer: 3 bonding pairs; 1 lone pair
parts.working: B1 3 bonding pairs; B1 1 lone pair (N has 5 outer electrons).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ammonia boils at −33 °C. Explain, in terms of forces, why ammonia has a low boiling point.
parts.answer: The intermolecular forces between ammonia molecules are weak, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.working: B1 weak intermolecular forces / forces between molecules; B1 little energy needed. Reject 'weak covalent bonds'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When iodine crystals are warmed gently in a boiling tube, a purple vapour forms. Name the type of structure in solid iodine.
parts.answer: simple molecular (simple covalent molecules of I₂)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why iodine changes to a vapour at a low temperature.
parts.answer: The forces between I₂ molecules are weak intermolecular forces, which need little energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 weak intermolecular forces; B1 little energy needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict whether solid iodine conducts electricity. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No, it has no ions or free electrons to carry charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many electrons are shared between the atoms in one molecule of carbon dioxide, O=C=O?
A 4
B 6
C 8
D 16
parts.answer: C 8
parts.working: There are two double bonds; each double bond is 2 shared pairs = 4 electrons, so 2 × 4 = 8. A counts only the number of shared pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the total number of covalent bonds in one molecule of methanol, CH₃OH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of non-bonding pairs of electrons on the oxygen atom in methanol.
parts.working: O has 6 outer electrons, 2 used in bonds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why liquid methanol does not conduct electricity.
parts.answer: It is made of neutral molecules; there are no ions or free (delocalised) electrons to carry charge.
parts.working: B1 molecules / no ions; B1 no mobile charged particles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A nitrogen molecule contains a triple bond. State the number of electrons shared between the two atoms and the number of non-bonding pairs on each nitrogen atom.
parts.answer: 6 shared electrons; 1 non-bonding pair on each N
parts.working: B1 6; B1 one lone pair each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student writes: 'When liquid nitrogen boils, the covalent bonds between the nitrogen atoms break.' Explain why this statement is incorrect.
parts.answer: Boiling only overcomes the weak intermolecular forces between N₂ molecules; the covalent (triple) bonds inside each molecule are not broken.
parts.working: B1 intermolecular forces overcome; B1 covalent bonds remain / N₂ molecules stay intact.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why nitrogen gas is very unreactive.
parts.answer: The N≡N triple bond is very strong and needs a lot of energy to break.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of diamond.
parts.answer: Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a giant three-dimensional (tetrahedral) lattice.
parts.working: B1 each C bonded to 4 others; B1 giant 3-D covalent lattice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the structure of diamond to explain why it is used in drill tips for oil wells.
parts.answer: It is very hard because of many strong covalent bonds in a giant structure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Graphite is used in pencils. Explain, in terms of its structure, why graphite is soft.
parts.answer: Graphite has layers of carbon atoms with weak forces between the layers, so the layers slide over each other.
parts.working: B1 layers; B1 weak forces between layers so layers slide.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂, is correct?
A It is made of separate SiO₂ molecules with weak forces between them.
B Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom to two silicon atoms.
C It conducts electricity when molten because it contains ions.
D It has a low melting point because the Si–O bonds are weak.
parts.answer: B Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom to two silicon atoms.
parts.working: SiO₂ is a giant covalent lattice: Si bonded to 4 O, each O to 2 Si, giving the 1 : 2 ratio. A describes a simple molecular structure like CO₂, which SiO₂ is not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
parts.answer: In graphite each carbon uses only three outer electrons in bonding, so one electron per atom is delocalised and can move; in diamond all four outer electrons are in covalent bonds.
parts.working: B1 graphite has delocalised / mobile electrons (one per C); B1 diamond: all 4 electrons used in bonds, none free.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one similarity in the structure of diamond and silicon(IV) oxide.
parts.answer: Both are giant covalent (macromolecular) structures with every atom held by strong covalent bonds in 3-D.
parts.working: Accept: both have tetrahedral arrangement around the central atom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why both diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have very high melting points.
parts.answer: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt them; this needs a lot of energy.
parts.working: B1 many strong covalent bonds; B1 must be broken, needing much energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe metallic bonding.
parts.answer: A lattice of positive metal ions in a 'sea' of delocalised electrons; held together by electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
parts.working: B1 lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons; B1 electrostatic attraction between them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why metals are good electrical conductors.
parts.answer: The delocalised electrons can move through the structure and carry charge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper is used for electrical wiring in houses. Explain in terms of structure why copper can be drawn into wires and why it conducts electricity.
parts.answer: Layers of copper ions can slide over each other (ductile); delocalised electrons move through the lattice and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 layers slide; B1 bonding not broken as layers slide / structure stays together; B1 delocalised electrons move.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why copper has a high melting point.
parts.answer: Strong electrostatic attraction between positive copper ions and delocalised electrons; much energy needed to overcome it.
parts.working: B1 strong attraction ions–electrons; B1 much energy needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why metals such as aluminium can be hammered into thin sheets (are malleable).
parts.answer: The layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons keep holding the structure together, so the metal changes shape without breaking.
parts.working: B1 layers of ions slide; B1 metallic bonding not broken / electrons still hold layers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The melting point of sodium is 98 °C and that of magnesium is 650 °C. Suggest why magnesium has the higher melting point.
parts.answer: Magnesium ions are Mg²⁺ (higher charge) and each atom gives two delocalised electrons, so the attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger.
parts.working: B1 Mg²⁺ / more delocalised electrons per atom; B1 stronger electrostatic attraction, more energy needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium chloride is a solid at room temperature but hydrogen chloride is a gas. State the type of bonding in each compound.
parts.answer: sodium chloride: ionic; hydrogen chloride: covalent

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in their states at room temperature.
parts.answer: Sodium chloride has a giant lattice with strong electrostatic attraction between ions, needing much energy to break; hydrogen chloride is made of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces, needing little energy to separate.
parts.working: B1 NaCl giant ionic lattice, strong forces between ions; B1 HCl simple molecules, weak intermolecular forces; B1 comparison of energy needed.

practice.stem:
Properties of four substances:
W: melting point 801 °C; conducts when solid: no; when molten: yes; dissolved in water: yes
X: melting point −95 °C; conducts when solid: no; when liquid: no; insoluble in water
Y: melting point 1083 °C; conducts when solid: yes; when molten: yes; insoluble in water
Z: melting point 1710 °C; conducts when solid: no; when molten: no; insoluble in water

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of structure in each of W, X, Y and Z. Choose from: giant ionic, simple molecular, giant metallic, giant covalent.
parts.answer: W giant ionic; X simple molecular; Y giant metallic; Z giant covalent

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why W conducts electricity when dissolved in water but not when solid.
