parts.answer: In solution its ions are free to move; in the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice.
parts.working: B1 ions move in solution; B1 ions fixed in solid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon and silicon are both in Group IV. Carbon dioxide turns directly to a gas at −78 °C, but silicon(IV) oxide melts at about 1700 °C. Explain this difference in terms of structure and bonding.
parts.answer: CO₂ is simple molecular: weak intermolecular forces between CO₂ molecules are overcome, needing little energy. SiO₂ is giant covalent: many strong covalent bonds between Si and O atoms must be broken, needing much energy.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ simple molecules; B1 weak intermolecular forces overcome; B1 SiO₂ giant covalent lattice; B1 strong covalent bonds broken.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether silicon(IV) oxide conducts electricity when molten. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No; it has no ions or delocalised electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a mixture?
A distilled water
B sea water
C sodium chloride
D copper
parts.answer: B sea water
parts.working: Sea water contains water with several dissolved salts that are not chemically combined, so it is a mixture. Distilled water and sodium chloride are compounds; copper is an element.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the formula of aluminium sulfate?
A AlSO₄
B Al₂SO₄
C Al(SO₄)₃
D Al₂(SO₄)₃
parts.answer: D Al₂(SO₄)₃
parts.working: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻: two Al³⁺ (+6) balance three SO₄²⁻ (−6), so Al₂(SO₄)₃. B ignores the charges.

practice.stem: Use these ions: Ca²⁺, Fe³⁺, Mg²⁺, NH₄⁺, OH⁻, O²⁻, CO₃²⁻, N³⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write the formula of each compound.
(i) calcium hydroxide
(ii) iron(III) oxide
(iii) ammonium carbonate
(iv) magnesium nitride
parts.answer: (i) Ca(OH)₂ (ii) Fe₂O₃ (iii) (NH₄)₂CO₃ (iv) Mg₃N₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many atoms are shown in the formula of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many atoms are shown in the formula of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·5H₂O?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many different elements are in ammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₃PO₄?
parts.answer: 4 (N, H, P, O)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Aqueous silver nitrate is added to aqueous sodium chloride. A white precipitate forms. Which is the ionic equation for this reaction?
A Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
B Na⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq) → NaNO₃(s)
C AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq)
D Ag(s) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(aq)
parts.answer: A Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
parts.working: The precipitate is silver chloride; Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions. C is the full (not ionic) equation; B shows a soluble salt as solid.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Balance this equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide:
Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂
parts.answer: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Balance this equation for the complete combustion of propane, the main fuel in LPG cylinders:
C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
parts.answer: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Balance this equation for aluminium burning in oxygen:
Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃
parts.answer: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Balance this equation and add state symbols for sodium reacting with water:
Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂
parts.answer: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)
parts.working: B1 balancing; B1 all state symbols.

practice.stem: Magnesium ribbon reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form aqueous magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced symbol equation, including state symbols, for this reaction.
parts.answer: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
parts.working: B1 formulae and balancing; B1 state symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g)
parts.working: B1 species; B1 balanced (charge and atoms).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the spectator ion in this reaction.
parts.answer: Chloride ion, Cl⁻

practice.stem: A student heats green copper(II) carbonate in a hard-glass test tube. The gas given off is bubbled through limewater.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two observations the student makes.
parts.answer: Green solid turns black; bubbles / gas given off (limewater turns milky).
parts.working: B1 green to black; B1 limewater milky / gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a balanced equation, with state symbols, for the decomposition.
parts.answer: CuCO₃(s) → CuO(s) + CO₂(g)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the delivery tube must be removed from the limewater before heating stops.
parts.answer: To stop limewater being sucked back into the hot tube (suck-back), which could crack it.

practice.stem: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate. A light blue precipitate forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the full balanced equation, with state symbols, for this reaction.
parts.answer: CuSO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) + Na₂SO₄(aq)
parts.working: B1 formulae and balancing; B1 state symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the formation of the blue precipitate.
parts.answer: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s)
parts.working: B1 species; B1 balanced with state symbols.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of any acid by any alkali.
parts.answer: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why sodium ions and sulfate ions do not appear in the ionic equation in (b).
parts.answer: They are spectator ions: they are in solution before and after the reaction and are not changed.

practice.stem: Roman numerals in a name show the oxidation number of an element.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of: (i) lead(II) nitrate (ii) chromium(III) oxide (iii) iron(II) sulfate
parts.answer: (i) Pb(NO₃)₂ (ii) Cr₂O₃ (iii) FeSO₄

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name: (i) KMnO₄ (ii) CuO (iii) Cl₂O
parts.answer: (i) potassium manganate(VII) (ii) copper(II) oxide (iii) chlorine(I) oxide

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Iron reacts with chlorine to form iron(III) chloride.
a Fe + b Cl₂ → c FeCl₃
Which values of a, b and c balance the equation?
A a = 1, b = 3, c = 1
B a = 2, b = 3, c = 2
C a = 2, b = 1, c = 2
D a = 1, b = 1, c = 1
parts.working: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃: 2 Fe and 6 Cl on each side. A has 6 Cl on the left but only 3 on the right.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles in 9.2 g of sodium.
parts.answer: 0.40 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

practice.stem:
In a lime kiln, calcium carbonate is heated strongly:
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
[Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of calcium oxide that can be made from 50 kg of pure calcium carbonate.
parts.answer: 28 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide released at the same time.
parts.answer: 22 kg

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the maximum mass of iron that can be made from 320 g of iron(III) oxide?
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
[Ar: O = 16, Fe = 56]
A 112 g
B 160 g
C 224 g
D 448 g
parts.answer: C 224 g
parts.working: Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160, so 320 g = 2.0 mol; 2 mol Fe₂O₃ → 4 mol Fe = 4 × 56 = 224 g. A forgets the 1:2 ratio.

practice.stem:
4.8 g of magnesium is added to dilute hydrochloric acid containing 0.30 mol of HCl.
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
[Ar: Mg = 24, Cl = 35.5]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show by calculation which reactant is in excess.
parts.answer: Mg: 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.20 mol needs 0.40 mol HCl; only 0.30 mol HCl, so magnesium is in excess.
parts.working: M1 moles Mg = 0.20; A1 Mg in excess with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of magnesium chloride formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of magnesium left unreacted.

practice.stem:
A student heated copper(II) carbonate in a crucible until there was no further change in mass.
Mass of empty crucible = 18.62 g
Mass of crucible + copper(II) carbonate = 21.10 g
Mass of crucible + solid after heating = 20.22 g
[Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Cu = 64]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of copper(II) carbonate used and the mass of copper(II) oxide formed.
parts.answer: CuCO₃ 2.48 g; CuO 1.60 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of each substance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the results support the equation CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂.
parts.answer: The mole ratio CuCO₃ : CuO is 1 : 1, as in the equation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the crucible was heated, cooled and weighed repeatedly until the mass stayed the same.
parts.answer: To make sure all the copper(II) carbonate had decomposed (reaction complete).

practice.stem: A sample of a hydrocarbon contains 2.4 g of carbon and 0.60 g of hydrogen. [Ar: H = 1, C = 12]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of the hydrocarbon.
parts.answer: CH₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: The relative molecular mass is 30. Deduce the molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₂H₆

practice.stem: A compound found in vinegar contains, by mass, 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen. [Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of the compound.
parts.answer: CH₂O
parts.working: M1 divide by Ar: C 3.33, H 6.7, O 3.33; M1 divide by smallest; A1 CH₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: The compound has Mr = 60 and turns blue litmus red. Deduce its molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₂H₄O₂ (ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH)

practice.stem:
Magnesium ribbon was heated in a crucible with a lid.
Mass of magnesium = 0.72 g
Mass of magnesium oxide formed = 1.20 g
[Ar: O = 16, Mg = 24]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen that combined with the magnesium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of magnesium oxide from these results.
parts.answer: MgO

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the lid was lifted slightly from time to time during heating.
parts.answer: To let oxygen (air) in so the magnesium can burn, while lifting it only slightly stops white magnesium oxide smoke escaping.
parts.working: B1 let air/oxygen in; B1 lid kept on to stop solid (oxide) escaping.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sample of an oxide of nitrogen contains 2.8 g of nitrogen and 6.4 g of oxygen. What is its empirical formula?
[Ar: N = 14, O = 16]
A NO
B NO₂
C N₂O
D N₂O₄
parts.answer: B NO₂
parts.working: N: 2.8 ÷ 14 = 0.20 mol; O: 6.4 ÷ 16 = 0.40 mol; ratio 1 : 2 → NO₂. N₂O₄ has the same ratio but is a molecular formula, not the simplest ratio.

practice.stem: A salt used in lawn treatments contains 36.8 % iron, 21.1 % sulfur and 42.1 % oxygen by mass. [Ar: H = 1, O = 16, S = 32, Fe = 56]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of the salt.
parts.answer: FeSO₄

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the salt. Include the oxidation number of iron.
parts.answer: Iron(II) sulfate

parts.label: c
parts.text: The salt forms green crystals with formula FeSO₄·7H₂O. Calculate its relative formula mass.

practice.stem: 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide, NaOH, is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³ of solution. [Ar: H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the solution in mol/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.40 mol/dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.
parts.answer: 16 g/dm³

practice.stem:
25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide was exactly neutralised by 21.40 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid.
H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of sulfuric acid used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide in 25.0 cm³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol/dm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.171 mol/dm³

practice.stem:
A student titrated 25.0 cm³ samples of diluted vinegar with 0.200 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide using phenolphthalein indicator.
Rough: initial 0.00 cm³, final 22.40 cm³
Titration 1: initial 0.50 cm³, final 22.15 cm³
Titration 2: initial 22.15 cm³, final 44.10 cm³
Titration 3: initial 1.20 cm³, final 22.85 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of NaOH used in the rough titration and in each of titrations 1, 2 and 3.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which results should be used to calculate the mean titre? Calculate the mean.
parts.answer: Titrations 1 and 3 (concordant, within 0.10 cm³); mean = 21.65 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Calculate the concentration of ethanoic acid in the diluted vinegar. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O
parts.answer: 0.173 mol/dm³

parts.label: d
parts.text: The vinegar had been diluted ten times. Calculate the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar in g/dm³. [Mr CH₃COOH = 60]
parts.answer: 104 g/dm³ (1.73 mol/dm³ × 60)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What volume of 0.50 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid is needed to react exactly with 2.0 g of calcium carbonate?
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
[Mr CaCO₃ = 100]
A 20 cm³
B 40 cm³
C 80 cm³
D 160 cm³
parts.answer: C 80 cm³
parts.working: Moles CaCO₃ = 0.020; HCl needed = 0.040 mol; volume = 0.040 ÷ 0.50 = 0.080 dm³ = 80 cm³. B forgets the 1:2 ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative formula mass of ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative formula mass of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the term 'relative formula mass' is used for calcium hydroxide rather than 'relative molecular mass'.
parts.answer: Calcium hydroxide is ionic, so it is not made of molecules.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the relative formula mass of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·5H₂O?
[Ar: H = 1, O = 16, S = 32, Cu = 64]
A 160
B 178
C 250
D 330
parts.working: CuSO₄ = 64 + 32 + 64 = 160; 5H₂O = 5 × 18 = 90; total 250. B adds only one H₂O.

practice.stem: Urea and ammonium nitrate are both sold to farmers in Pakistan as nitrogen fertilisers. [Ar: H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define relative atomic mass, Ar.
parts.answer: The average mass of the isotopes of an element (weighted by abundance) compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
parts.working: B1 average/weighted mass of isotopes; B1 relative to 1/12 of carbon-12.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative formula mass of urea, CO(NH₂)₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in urea and in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃ (Mr = 80). State which fertiliser supplies more nitrogen per kilogram.
parts.answer: Urea 46.7 %; ammonium nitrate 35.0 %; urea supplies more.

practice.stem: One mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 0.25 mol of carbon dioxide at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.).
parts.answer: 6.0 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of oxygen in 600 cm³ of oxygen gas at r.t.p.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of 1.2 dm³ of methane, CH₄, at r.t.p. [Ar: H = 1, C = 12]

practice.stem: [Ar: Mg = 24; molar gas volume = 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³ at r.t.p., formed when 0.60 g of magnesium reacts with excess dilute sulfuric acid.
Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂
parts.answer: 600 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student collected only 540 cm³ of hydrogen. Suggest one reason for this.
parts.answer: Some gas escaped before the bung was put in / leaks / the magnesium was not pure (had an oxide coating).

practice.stem:
A student added a small piece of marble (calcium carbonate) to excess dilute hydrochloric acid and collected the carbon dioxide in a gas syringe. When the reaction stopped the syringe contained 96 cm³ of gas at r.t.p.
[Mr CaCO₃ = 100; molar gas volume = 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of carbon dioxide collected.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate that reacted.
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: In a separate experiment, 20 cm³ of methane is burned completely: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the volume of oxygen needed and the volume of carbon dioxide formed, both at r.t.p.
parts.answer: 40 cm³ oxygen; 20 cm³ carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 each (equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of moles).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a gas syringe gives a more accurate volume of carbon dioxide than collecting it over water in an upturned measuring cylinder.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is slightly soluble in water, so some would dissolve.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which salt is insoluble in water?
A sodium carbonate
B barium sulfate
C copper(II) nitrate
D potassium chloride
parts.answer: B barium sulfate
parts.working: Barium sulfate is one of the insoluble sulfates (with calcium and lead sulfates). All sodium and potassium salts and all nitrates are soluble.

practice.stem: A student makes crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate by adding excess copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: copper(II) oxide + sulfuric acid → copper(II) sulfate + water

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why copper(II) oxide is added in excess.
parts.answer: To make sure all the acid has reacted (so the salt is not contaminated with acid).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the excess copper(II) oxide is removed.
parts.answer: Filtration; it stays on the filter paper as the residue.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate are then obtained from the filtrate.
parts.answer: Heat the filtrate to evaporate some water until the crystallisation point (crystals form on a cold glass rod); leave to cool so crystals form; filter off the crystals and dry them between filter papers.
parts.working: B1 heat/evaporate to crystallisation point; B1 cool; B1 filter and dry.

practice.stem: A student adds zinc carbonate powder, a little at a time, to dilute hydrochloric acid to make zinc chloride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: ZnCO₃ + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is seen as the zinc carbonate is added.
parts.answer: Fizzing / bubbles; the white solid disappears.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the student knows that the zinc carbonate is in excess.
parts.answer: Fizzing stops and solid remains in the beaker.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the mixture is filtered before crystallising.
parts.answer: To remove the excess (unreacted) zinc carbonate.

practice.stem: State whether each salt is soluble or insoluble in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: sodium carbonate
parts.answer: Soluble

parts.label: b
parts.text: calcium carbonate
parts.answer: Insoluble

parts.label: c
parts.text: silver chloride
parts.answer: Insoluble

parts.label: d
parts.text: ammonium sulfate
parts.answer: Soluble

parts.label: e
parts.text: lead(II) nitrate
parts.answer: Soluble

parts.label: f
parts.text: calcium sulfate
parts.answer: Insoluble

practice.stem: A student makes zinc sulfate crystals by adding excess granulated zinc to dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the student sees when the zinc is added to the acid.
parts.answer: Fizzing / bubbles; zinc gets smaller.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a test to identify the gas produced.
parts.answer: Lighted splint pops.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the student can tell that the reaction has finished.
parts.answer: Bubbling stops and some zinc remains.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂
parts.working: B1 formulae; B1 correct and balanced.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain why the solution should not be heated to dryness to obtain the crystals.
parts.answer: The water of crystallisation would be lost (crystals would not be hydrated) / the salt may decompose or spit.

practice.stem: Barium sulfate is an insoluble salt used in medical X-ray imaging.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two aqueous solutions that could be mixed to make barium sulfate.
parts.answer: e.g. aqueous barium nitrate (or barium chloride) and aqueous sodium sulfate (or dilute sulfuric acid).
parts.working: B1 soluble barium salt; B1 soluble sulfate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of barium sulfate.
parts.answer: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how a pure, dry sample of barium sulfate is obtained from the mixture.
parts.answer: Filter; wash the residue with distilled water; dry it (in a warm oven / between filter papers).
parts.working: B1 filter; B1 wash with distilled water; B1 dry.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the method of preparation used.
parts.answer: Precipitation

practice.stem: Potassium nitrate is used in fertilisers. It can be made from aqueous potassium hydroxide and dilute nitric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why potassium nitrate cannot be made by adding an excess of a solid to the acid and filtering.
parts.answer: Potassium hydroxide (and all potassium compounds) are soluble, so any excess cannot be removed by filtering.
parts.working: B1 KOH soluble; B1 excess cannot be filtered off.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a titration is used to make a pure solution of potassium nitrate.
parts.answer: Pipette 25.0 cm³ of KOH(aq) into a flask with a few drops of indicator; add nitric acid from a burette until the indicator just changes colour; record the volume; repeat with the same volumes of acid and alkali but no indicator.
parts.working: B1 pipette alkali + indicator; B1 add acid from burette to end-point; B1 note volume; B1 repeat without indicator.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: KOH + HNO₃ → KNO₃ + H₂O

practice.stem:
A student heats hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄·xH₂O, in a crucible, cools and reweighs it, and repeats until the mass is constant.
Mass of empty crucible = 21.40 g
Mass of crucible + hydrated salt = 26.32 g
Mass of crucible + salt after heating to constant mass = 23.80 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of hydrated salt used and the mass of water lost.
parts.answer: Hydrated salt 4.92 g; water 2.52 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of water in the hydrated salt. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use Mr MgSO₄ = 120 and Mr H₂O = 18 to find x.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the student heated the crucible to constant mass.
parts.answer: To make sure all the water of crystallisation had been driven off.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which method is most suitable for preparing a sample of silver chloride?
A titration of an acid with an alkali
B adding excess metal to an acid and filtering
C mixing two aqueous solutions to form a precipitate
D adding excess carbonate to an acid and filtering
parts.answer: C mixing two aqueous solutions to form a precipitate
parts.working: Silver chloride is insoluble, so it is made by precipitation, e.g. aqueous silver nitrate + aqueous sodium chloride. Methods A, B and D make soluble salts; silver does not react with dilute acids anyway.

practice.stem: Some salts form crystals that contain water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the meaning of the term hydrated, as used for a salt.
parts.answer: A salt that contains water of crystallisation (water chemically bonded in the crystal).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction when water is added to anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride to form CoCl₂·6H₂O. Use the correct arrow.
parts.answer: CoCl₂ + 6H₂O ⇌ CoCl₂·6H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour change seen when water is added to anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride.
parts.answer: Blue to pink

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how this change can be used as a test for water.
parts.answer: If a liquid turns blue cobalt(II) chloride paper pink, it contains water.

practice.stem: 2.50 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, is heated until no more water is lost. 1.60 g of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate remains. Mr: CuSO₄ = 160, H₂O = 18.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of water lost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the value of x.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the colour change on heating.
parts.answer: Blue to white

practice.stem:
A student reacts 4.0 g of copper(II) oxide with excess dilute sulfuric acid and crystallises hydrated copper(II) sulfate.
CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O, then CuSO₄ + 5H₂O → CuSO₄·5H₂O
Mr: CuO = 80, CuSO₄·5H₂O = 250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of CuSO₄·5H₂O that can be made.
parts.working: M1 mol CuO = 4.0 ÷ 80 = 0.050 = mol CuSO₄·5H₂O; A1 × 250 = 12.5 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student obtains 9.8 g of crystals. Calculate the percentage yield.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the yield is less than 100%.
parts.answer: Some copper(II) sulfate stays dissolved in the solution left after crystallising / losses during filtering and transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
When 4.30 g of hydrated calcium sulfate, CaSO₄·xH₂O, is heated to constant mass, 3.40 g of anhydrous CaSO₄ remains. Mr: CaSO₄ = 136, H₂O = 18. What is the value of x?
A 1
B 2
C 5
D 10
parts.answer: B 2
parts.working: mol CaSO₄ = 3.40 ÷ 136 = 0.0250; mol H₂O = 0.90 ÷ 18 = 0.0500; ratio 1 : 2, so x = 2. C (5) is the value for copper(II) sulfate crystals, not for this salt.

practice.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ aqueous sodium hydroxide is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of dilute sulfuric acid. Mr: Na₂SO₄ = 142.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid in mol/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.125 mol/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium sulfate in the neutral solution.

practice.stem: Washing soda crystals are sold in markets as a cleaning agent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to find the value of x in washing soda, Na₂CO₃·xH₂O, a hydrated salt. Include how you would use your results. You may use common laboratory apparatus.
parts.answer: Weigh crucible, add salt, heat to constant mass, calculate moles ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: weigh an empty crucible; add a known mass of washing soda (e.g. 3 g) and reweigh; heat (gently, then strongly) with a Bunsen burner on a pipe-clay triangle; cool (in a desiccator) and reweigh; repeat heating, cooling and weighing until the mass is constant; mass of water = loss in mass; mol Na₂CO₃ = mass of residue ÷ 106 and mol H₂O = mass lost ÷ 18; x = mol H₂O ÷ mol Na₂CO₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the colour of methyl orange in aqueous sodium hydroxide?
A red
B orange
C yellow
D blue
parts.answer: C yellow
parts.working: Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali. Blue is the colour of thymolphthalein (or litmus) in alkali.

practice.stem: Name the products formed when dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with each substance. For (a) and (b) also give one observation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: magnesium
parts.answer: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen; fizzing/bubbles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: calcium carbonate
parts.answer: Calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide; fizzing/bubbles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: sodium hydroxide solution
parts.answer: Sodium chloride and water

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the name given to the reaction in (c).
parts.answer: Neutralisation

practice.stem: A student tests household vinegar with different indicators.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of litmus, methyl orange and thymolphthalein in vinegar (an acid).
parts.answer: Litmus red; methyl orange red; thymolphthalein colourless
parts.working: B1 each. Methyl orange: accept red or orange-red (vinegar is only weakly acidic, pH about 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student dips red litmus paper into vinegar and sees no change. Explain why this does not show that vinegar is an acid.
parts.answer: Red litmus stays red in acid and in neutral solutions; only blue litmus turning red shows an acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name an indicator that would give the approximate pH of the vinegar.
parts.answer: Universal indicator

practice.stem: Water can act as an acid or as a base.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define an acid and a base in terms of proton transfer.
parts.answer: An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a base is a proton acceptor.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻
Identify the acid and the base in the forward reaction. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Water is the acid (donates H⁺); ammonia is the base (accepts H⁺).
parts.working: B1 identification; B1 explanation in terms of H⁺.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
HCl + NH₃ → NH₄Cl
Which substance acts as a base in this reaction?
parts.answer: Ammonia

practice.stem: A mixture of solid ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide is warmed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gas produced.
parts.answer: Ammonia

parts.label: b
parts.text: Complete the equation: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + ___ + ___
parts.answer: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the test for this gas.
parts.answer: Turns damp red litmus paper blue.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why farmers should not spread calcium hydroxide on soil at the same time as an ammonium fertiliser.
parts.answer: The base reacts with the ammonium salt, releasing ammonia gas, so nitrogen is lost from the soil (fertiliser is wasted).
parts.working: B1 ammonia released; B1 nitrogen lost.

practice.stem: A farmer in the Swat valley tests his soil and finds pH 4.5, which is too acidic for the crops he wants to grow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name a substance that the farmer could add to raise the pH of the soil.
parts.answer: Calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) or calcium oxide (lime) or calcium carbonate (limestone)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali.
parts.answer: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of ions, why the pH of the soil increases.
parts.answer: The base removes H⁺ ions from the soil (forming water), so the concentration of H⁺ ions decreases.
parts.working: B1 H⁺ removed/react; B1 lower H⁺ concentration.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the farmer should not add too much of the substance.
parts.answer: The soil would become alkaline, which is also bad for crops.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which oxide is amphoteric?
A zinc oxide
B calcium oxide
C sulfur dioxide
D carbon monoxide
parts.answer: A zinc oxide
parts.working: Zinc oxide reacts with both acids and alkalis to form a salt and water. Calcium oxide is basic, sulfur dioxide is acidic, carbon monoxide is neutral.

practice.stem: A teacher burns magnesium and sulfur separately in oxygen. Each product is shaken with water containing universal indicator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of universal indicator in the solution from magnesium oxide, and suggest its pH.
parts.answer: Blue/purple; pH about 10 (accept 8–11).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour of universal indicator in the solution from sulfur dioxide, and suggest its pH.
parts.answer: Red/orange; pH about 3 (accept 1–5).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the general rule linking the type of element to the type of oxide.
parts.answer: Metals form basic oxides; non-metals form acidic oxides.

practice.stem: Classify each oxide as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral.

parts.label: a
parts.text: magnesium oxide
parts.answer: Basic

parts.label: b
parts.text: sulfur dioxide
parts.answer: Acidic

parts.label: c
parts.text: aluminium oxide
parts.answer: Amphoteric

parts.label: d
parts.text: carbon monoxide
parts.answer: Neutral

parts.label: e
parts.text: phosphorus(V) oxide
parts.answer: Acidic

practice.stem: Aluminium oxide is described as an amphoteric oxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term amphoteric.
parts.answer: Reacts with both acids and bases to form a salt and water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of aluminium oxide with hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what you would do to show that aluminium oxide also behaves as an acidic oxide, and what you would see.
parts.answer: Add (warm) aqueous sodium hydroxide; the white solid dissolves (to form a salt, sodium aluminate, and water).
parts.working: B1 add NaOH(aq); B1 solid dissolves.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the oxide of a metal such as magnesium does not dissolve in aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Magnesium oxide is basic, so it does not react with bases/alkalis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Oxide W does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid or with aqueous sodium hydroxide. What is W?
A carbon monoxide
B carbon dioxide
C zinc oxide
D copper(II) oxide
parts.answer: A carbon monoxide
parts.working: Carbon monoxide is a neutral oxide. Carbon dioxide is acidic (reacts with NaOH), zinc oxide is amphoteric (reacts with both), copper(II) oxide is basic (reacts with HCl).

practice.stem: Universal indicator shows the pH of a solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Match each substance to its likely pH: stomach acid, lemon juice, pure water, oven cleaner. pH values: 1, 3, 7, 13.
parts.answer: Stomach acid 1; lemon juice 3; pure water 7; oven cleaner 13
parts.working: B2 all four correct; B1 two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the ion present in excess in all alkaline solutions.
parts.answer: Hydroxide ion, OH⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how universal indicator paper is used to find the pH of a solution.
parts.answer: Dip a glass rod in the solution and touch it on the paper (or dip the paper); compare the colour with the pH colour chart.
parts.working: B1 apply solution; B1 compare with colour chart.

practice.stem: A student has 0.10 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid and 0.10 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest which acid has the higher pH.
parts.answer: Ethanoic acid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in pH in terms of ions.
parts.answer: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid and is fully dissociated into ions; ethanoic acid is weak and only partially dissociated, so its H⁺ ion concentration is lower.
parts.working: B1 strong = fully dissociated; B1 weak = partially, lower [H⁺].

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the dissociation of ethanoic acid in water.
parts.answer: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺

parts.label: d
parts.text: Magnesium ribbon is added to each acid. State how the rate of reaction compares.
parts.answer: Faster with hydrochloric acid (more H⁺ ions per unit volume).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which solution has the lowest pH?
A 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid
B 0.1 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid
C 0.01 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid
D 0.1 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide
parts.answer: A 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid
parts.working: Lowest pH = highest H⁺ concentration. HCl is fully dissociated; at 0.1 mol/dm³ it has more H⁺ than the same concentration of weak ethanoic acid (partly dissociated) and than the more dilute HCl. NaOH is alkaline.

practice.stem:
Three acids, P, Q and R, all at 0.50 mol/dm³ and in excess, each react with 0.12 g of magnesium ribbon.
Acid: P, Q, R
pH: 0.3, 2.5, 0.3
Volume of hydrogen after 60 s / cm³: 92, 21, 95

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which acids are strong? Explain your choice using the data.
parts.answer: Acids P and R; they have the lowest pH and give the most hydrogen in 60 s, showing a higher concentration of H⁺ ions.
parts.working: B1 P and R; B1 reason from data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why acid Q gives less gas in 60 s.
parts.answer: Q is weak/partially dissociated, so there is a lower concentration of H⁺ ions, so fewer collisions per unit time between H⁺ ions and magnesium.
parts.working: B1 lower [H⁺]; B1 less frequent collisions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: All the magnesium eventually reacts in each acid. Explain why the final volume of hydrogen is the same in each case.
parts.answer: The acid is in excess and the same mass of magnesium is used, so the same number of moles of hydrogen is formed (as Q dissociates further as H⁺ is used up).
parts.working: B1 same amount of Mg / Mg limiting; B1 same moles of H₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the name of the main ore of aluminium?
A bauxite
B cryolite
C hematite
D limestone
parts.answer: A bauxite
parts.working: Aluminium is extracted from bauxite (impure aluminium oxide). Cryolite is the solvent used in the electrolysis; hematite is an iron ore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three solid raw materials added at the top of the blast furnace.
parts.answer: Hematite (iron ore), coke (carbon), limestone.
parts.working: 2 marks all three; 1 mark for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write equations for: (i) carbon burning in hot air to form carbon dioxide; (ii) carbon dioxide reacting with more carbon to form carbon monoxide; (iii) carbon monoxide reducing iron(III) oxide.
parts.answer: (i) C + O₂ → CO₂ (ii) CO₂ + C → 2CO (iii) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the reaction in (i) is important for the working of the furnace.
parts.answer: It is exothermic and heats the furnace.

practice.stem: Five metals: aluminium, copper, gold, iron, potassium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which metal is found uncombined (native) in the ground?
parts.answer: Gold

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which two metals must be extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds?
parts.answer: Potassium and aluminium

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which two metals can be extracted by heating their oxides with carbon?
parts.answer: Iron and copper (copper also from its sulfide ores)

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the link between the position of a metal in the reactivity series and its method of extraction.
parts.answer: The more reactive the metal, the harder it is to extract; metals above carbon need electrolysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why is limestone added to the blast furnace?
A It reduces iron(III) oxide to iron.
B It decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with silicon dioxide impurities to form slag.
C It burns to provide heat for the furnace.
D It lowers the melting point of the iron ore.
parts.answer: B It decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with silicon dioxide impurities to form slag.
parts.working: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO (basic) + SiO₂ (acidic) → CaSiO₃ (slag). Carbon monoxide, not limestone, reduces the ore (A).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted by heating aluminium oxide with carbon.
parts.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove the oxygen from aluminium oxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite.
parts.answer: This lowers the operating temperature (aluminium oxide has a very high melting point), saving energy, and lets the ions move.
parts.working: B1 lowers temperature/ melting point; B1 saves energy/cost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the carbon anodes have to be replaced regularly.
parts.answer: Oxygen is formed at the anode; at the high temperature it reacts with the carbon to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes burn away.
parts.working: B1 oxygen produced at anode; B1 reacts with carbon to form CO₂.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
parts.answer: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al

practice.stem: A steel works near Karachi uses an iron ore that contains 80 % iron(III) oxide by mass; the rest is mainly silicon dioxide. [Ar: O = 16, Fe = 56]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iron(III) oxide in 1000 tonnes of the ore.
parts.answer: 800 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Calculate the maximum mass of iron that can be produced from 1000 tonnes of the ore.
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
parts.answer: 560 tonnes
parts.working: M1 Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160, contains 112 of Fe; A1 800 × 112 ÷ 160 = 560 t

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the formation of slag.
parts.answer: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃

practice.stem: A student reduces 3.20 g of copper(II) oxide by heating it in a horizontal glass tube while a stream of hydrogen passes over it. Excess hydrogen is burned at a small hole at the far end of the tube. [Ar: O = 16, Cu = 64]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the colour change seen in the tube.
parts.answer: Black solid turns pink-brown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why hydrogen is passed through the tube for a while before heating starts.
parts.answer: To push out all the air; a mixture of hydrogen and air could explode when heated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why hydrogen is kept flowing while the tube cools.
parts.answer: To stop the hot copper reacting with oxygen in the air and turning back into copper(II) oxide.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of copper(II) oxide used and the mass of copper expected.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction and state which substance is reduced.
parts.answer: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O; copper(II) oxide is reduced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iron from the blast furnace contains about 4 % carbon. State one property of this iron that makes it unsuitable for most uses.
parts.answer: It is brittle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how this iron is converted into steel. Include the role of oxygen and of calcium oxide.
parts.answer: Oxygen is blown into the molten iron; it oxidises carbon to carbon monoxide/carbon dioxide gas which escapes; it also oxidises impurities such as silicon and phosphorus to acidic oxides; calcium oxide (a basic oxide) is added and reacts with these acidic oxides to form slag, which is removed.
parts.working: B1 oxygen blown into molten iron; B1 carbon removed as CO/CO₂; B1 impurities form acidic oxides; B1 CaO neutralises them to form slag.

practice.stem: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite. [Ar: O = 16, Al = 27]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the anode.
parts.answer: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of aluminium that can be obtained from 51 tonnes of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.
parts.answer: 27 tonnes
parts.working: M1 Mr Al₂O₃ = 102, Al = 54 per formula; A1 51 × 54 ÷ 102 = 27 t

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the process is described as a redox reaction.
parts.answer: Aluminium ions gain electrons (reduction) at the cathode; oxide ions lose electrons (oxidation) at the anode.
parts.working: B1 reduction at cathode; B1 oxidation at anode.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why aluminium smelters are often built near hydroelectric power stations.
parts.answer: Electrolysis needs very large amounts of electricity; hydroelectric power is cheap (and renewable).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the oxidation number of iron in Fe₂O₃ and in Fe.
parts.answer: +3 in Fe₂O₃; 0 in Fe

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the oxidation number of carbon in CO and in CO₂.
parts.answer: +2 in CO; +4 in CO₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent in the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Explain.
parts.answer: Fe₂O₃ is the oxidising agent (iron's oxidation number decreases; it is reduced); CO is the reducing agent (carbon's oxidation number increases; it is oxidised).
parts.working: B1 Fe₂O₃ oxidising agent with reason; B1 CO reducing agent with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The overall reaction in the cell is 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. Calculate the number of moles of oxygen formed when 108 kg of aluminium is produced.
parts.answer: 3000 mol (3 kmol)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume all the oxygen reacts with the carbon anode to form carbon dioxide: C + O₂ → CO₂. Calculate the mass of carbon used, in kg.
parts.answer: 36 kg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one environmental problem caused by this anode reaction.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas / contributes to climate change.

practice.stem:
A student heated a mixture of each metal oxide with powdered carbon in a crucible for ten minutes.
Copper(II) oxide: pink-brown solid formed
Lead(II) oxide: silvery beads of metal formed
Magnesium oxide: no change
Aluminium oxide: no change
[Ar: O = 16, Pb = 207]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to place carbon in the reactivity series relative to copper, lead, magnesium and aluminium.
parts.answer: Order (most reactive first): magnesium/aluminium > carbon > lead > copper
parts.working: B1 carbon above lead and copper; B1 carbon below magnesium and aluminium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of lead that could be obtained from 2.23 g of lead(II) oxide, PbO.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of lead(II) oxide with carbon, forming carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: 2PbO + C → 2Pb + CO₂

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why aluminium oxide gave no reaction with carbon.
parts.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce its oxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A metal reacts vigorously with cold water, floats and moves about on the surface, and gives off hydrogen. Which metal could it be?
A copper
B iron
C sodium
D zinc
parts.answer: C sodium
parts.working: Only Group I metals such as sodium react vigorously with cold water. Zinc and iron react only with steam (iron slowly); copper does not react.

practice.stem:
Observations:
Calcium: fizzes steadily in cold water.
Magnesium: very slow reaction with cold water; burns brightly when heated in steam.
Iron: no reaction with cold water; reacts slowly when heated strongly in steam.
Copper: no reaction with water or steam.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put the four metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first.
parts.answer: Calcium, magnesium, iron, copper
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark one pair swapped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas formed when calcium reacts with water and describe a test for it.
parts.answer: Hydrogen; a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the word equation for magnesium reacting with steam.
parts.answer: magnesium + steam → magnesium oxide + hydrogen

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mixture would react?
A copper + magnesium sulfate solution
B zinc + copper(II) sulfate solution
C silver + iron(II) sulfate solution
D iron + zinc sulfate solution
parts.answer: B zinc + copper(II) sulfate solution
parts.working: A metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt. Zinc is above copper. In A, C and D the metal is less reactive than the metal in the salt.

practice.stem:
Each metal was added to solutions of the nitrates of the other metals. ✓ = reaction, ✗ = no reaction.
Metal W: with X nitrate ✓, with Y nitrate ✗, with Z nitrate ✓
Metal X: with W nitrate ✗, with Y nitrate ✗, with Z nitrate ✗
Metal Y: with W nitrate ✓, with X nitrate ✓, with Z nitrate ✓
Metal Z: with W nitrate ✗, with X nitrate ✓, with Y nitrate ✗

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to put metals W, X, Y and Z in order of reactivity, most reactive first.
parts.answer: Y, W, Z, X

parts.label: b
parts.text: Metal Y is magnesium and metal X is copper. Write the ionic equation for the reaction of magnesium with copper(II) ions.
parts.answer: Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
parts.working: B1 species; B1 balanced with state symbols.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the reaction in (b), state which species is oxidised. Explain in terms of electrons.
parts.answer: Magnesium is oxidised because it loses electrons (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻).

practice.stem:
Equal masses of four metal powders were added separately to 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. The volume of hydrogen collected in a gas syringe in the first 60 seconds was recorded.
Magnesium: 48 cm³
Zinc: 21 cm³
Iron: 6 cm³
Copper: 0 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of gas production, in cm³/s, for magnesium, zinc and iron.
parts.answer: Mg 0.80 cm³/s; Zn 0.35 cm³/s; Fe 0.10 cm³/s

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the order of reactivity shown by the results.
parts.answer: Magnesium > zinc > iron > copper

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why copper gave no gas.
parts.answer: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that must be controlled.
parts.answer: Mass/surface area of metal; volume and concentration of acid; temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the order of reactivity of metals in terms of their ions.
parts.answer: More reactive metals lose electrons more easily to form positive ions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, yet aluminium cooking pots do not react with water. Explain why.
parts.answer: Aluminium is covered by a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide which protects the metal underneath.
parts.working: B1 oxide layer; B1 prevents contact / unreactive.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An iron nail is placed in aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Describe two observations and write the ionic equation.
parts.answer: Pink-brown copper coats the nail; blue solution fades (turns pale green). Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
parts.working: B1 copper deposit; B1 colour change; B1 equation.

practice.stem: A metal M forms M²⁺ ions. M displaces iron from aqueous iron(II) sulfate but does not react with aqueous zinc sulfate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of M with iron(II) ions.
parts.answer: M(s) + Fe²⁺(aq) → M²⁺(aq) + Fe(s)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Place M in the reactivity series relative to zinc, iron and copper.
parts.answer: Zinc > M > iron > copper

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict whether M would react when heated with copper(II) oxide. Explain.
parts.answer: Yes; M is more reactive than copper so it removes oxygen from copper(II) oxide.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict whether the oxide of M could be reduced by heating it with carbon. Explain.
parts.answer: Yes; M is below zinc (which can be extracted with carbon), so M is less reactive than carbon.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substances must both be present for iron to rust?
A oxygen and water
B carbon dioxide and water
C nitrogen and oxygen
D oxygen and salt
parts.answer: A oxygen and water
parts.working: Rusting needs both oxygen and water. Salt speeds rusting up but is not needed.

practice.stem:
Four identical iron nails were set up for one week:
Tube A: nail in tap water, open to air. Mass increase 0.12 g.
Tube B: nail in boiled water with a layer of oil on top. Mass increase 0.00 g.
Tube C: nail in air with anhydrous calcium chloride, stoppered. Mass increase 0.00 g.
Tube D: nail in salt water, open to air. Mass increase 0.21 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In which tubes did the nails rust?
parts.answer: Tubes A and D

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the nail in tube B did not rust.
parts.answer: Boiling removes dissolved oxygen (air); the oil layer stops oxygen dissolving back in.
parts.working: B1 boiling removes oxygen; B1 oil stops air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the nail in tube C did not rust.
parts.answer: Anhydrous calcium chloride absorbs water vapour, so the air is dry.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the mass increase was in tube D than in tube A. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.8 times

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest why car bodies rust faster in coastal cities such as Karachi.
parts.answer: Salt (sodium chloride) from sea spray speeds up rusting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how painting a steel gate prevents rusting.
parts.answer: It forms a barrier that keeps water and oxygen away from the iron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the metal used to galvanise steel roof sheets.
parts.answer: Zinc

parts.label: c
parts.text: A galvanised roof sheet is scratched, exposing the steel. Explain why the steel still does not rust.
parts.answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes/is oxidised instead of the iron (sacrificial protection).
parts.working: B1 zinc more reactive; B1 zinc oxidised in preference to iron.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a scratched painted gate does rust.
parts.answer: The paint is only a barrier; once broken, water and oxygen reach the iron.

practice.stem: Blocks of zinc are bolted to the steel hulls of ships in Karachi port, below the waterline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of protection given by the blocks.
parts.answer: Sacrificial protection

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction of the zinc blocks and explain why it protects the steel.
parts.answer: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻; zinc loses electrons more easily than iron, so it is oxidised instead of the iron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An engineer suggests using copper blocks instead. Explain why this would not work.
parts.answer: Copper is less reactive than iron, so the iron would be oxidised instead (rusting faster).
parts.working: B1 copper less reactive; B1 iron corrodes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the chemical name of rust.
parts.answer: Hydrated iron(III) oxide

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain why the zinc blocks must be replaced from time to time.
parts.answer: They are used up as the zinc corrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Overhead power cables are made of aluminium wrapped round a steel core. Which properties make aluminium suitable?
A high density and good electrical conductivity
B low density and good electrical conductivity
C low density and poor electrical conductivity
D high melting point and magnetic
parts.answer: B low density and good electrical conductivity
parts.working: Aluminium conducts electricity well and has a low density, so the cables are light. The steel core adds strength.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three physical properties of metals.
parts.answer: Good conductors of heat; good conductors of electricity; malleable; ductile; high melting/boiling points; shiny.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Metals react with oxygen to form oxides. State the type of oxide formed by most metals and how it reacts with acids.
parts.answer: Basic oxides; they react with acids to form a salt and water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one physical property in which non-metals generally differ from metals.
parts.answer: Poor conductors / brittle when solid / low melting points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper is used for electrical wiring in houses. Give two properties of copper that make it suitable.
parts.answer: Good electrical conductor; ductile (can be drawn into wires).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aluminium is used to make aircraft bodies. Give two reasons.
parts.answer: Low density; strong (as an alloy); resists corrosion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Aluminium is also used for food containers and foil. Explain why it does not corrode easily.
parts.answer: It has a protective oxide layer.

practice.stem:
Data for four metals:
Metal P: density 2.7 g/cm³, relative electrical conductivity 61, melting point 660 °C, resists corrosion, low cost
Metal Q: density 8.9 g/cm³, relative electrical conductivity 100, melting point 1085 °C, resists corrosion, medium cost
Metal R: density 7.9 g/cm³, relative electrical conductivity 17, melting point 1538 °C, rusts, very low cost
Metal S: density 4.5 g/cm³, relative electrical conductivity 4, melting point 1668 °C, resists corrosion, high cost

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of a 500 cm³ bracket made of each metal.
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark two or three (mass = density × volume).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which metal would be best for electrical cables carried on pylons? Explain using the data.
parts.answer: P; good conductivity and lowest density (and cheap) so cables are light.
parts.working: B1 P; B1 reason using data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which metal would be best for a part of a jet engine that becomes very hot and must stay strong? Explain.
parts.answer: S; highest melting point, does not corrode and fairly low density.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why Q is used for house wiring even though it is more dense than P.
parts.answer: It is a better electrical conductor (thinner wires can be used).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define an alloy.
parts.answer: A mixture of a metal with other elements (metals or non-metals).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an alloy is usually harder and stronger than the pure metal it is made from.
parts.answer: In the pure metal, atoms are the same size and arranged in layers that slide easily; in the alloy, atoms of different sizes disrupt the layers; so the layers cannot slide over each other easily.
parts.working: B1 pure metal layers slide; B1 different-sized atoms in alloy; B1 layers can no longer slide easily.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one use of brass and the property it depends on.
parts.answer: Musical instruments / door fittings / electrical plugs – hard and resists corrosion (or attractive).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which metals are mixed to make brass?
A copper and tin
B copper and zinc
C iron and carbon
D iron and chromium
parts.answer: B copper and zinc
parts.working: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Copper and tin make bronze (A).

practice.stem: The city of Sialkot exports surgical instruments made of stainless steel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the main metal in stainless steel and two other elements added to it.
parts.answer: Iron; chromium and nickel (and a little carbon).
parts.working: B1 iron; B1 two of chromium, nickel, carbon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chromium and the mass of nickel in a 250 g instrument made of 18/8 stainless steel (18 % chromium and 8 % nickel by mass).
parts.answer: Chromium 45 g; nickel 20 g

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why stainless steel, rather than mild steel, is chosen for surgical instruments.
parts.answer: Stainless steel resists corrosion (does not rust) and is hard/strong; instruments must stay clean and can be sterilised repeatedly.
parts.working: B1 resists corrosion; B1 link to use (hygiene/sterilising).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one use of mild steel.
parts.answer: Car bodies / machinery / building girders.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property is typical of transition elements?
A low melting point
B low density
C they form coloured compounds
D they react vigorously with cold water
parts.answer: C they form coloured compounds
parts.working: Transition elements form coloured compounds, have high densities and high melting points. D describes Group I metals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three properties of transition elements that are not shown by Group I metals.
parts.answer: Any three of: high density; high melting point; form coloured compounds; act as catalysts (elements or compounds); have variable oxidation numbers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the transition element used as the catalyst in the Haber process.
parts.answer: iron

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which the physical properties of iron differ from those of sodium.
parts.answer: Iron has a higher melting point; iron has a higher density.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept: iron is harder / stronger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Iron forms two chlorides, FeCl₂ and FeCl₃. Name each chloride, using Roman numerals.
parts.answer: FeCl₂ iron(II) chloride; FeCl₃ iron(III) chloride

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which property of transition elements is shown by the existence of these two chlorides?
parts.answer: They have variable oxidation numbers (more than one oxidation state).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the formula of iron(III) sulfate?
A FeSO₄
B Fe₃SO₄
C Fe₂(SO₄)₃
D Fe(SO₄)₃
parts.answer: C Fe₂(SO₄)₃
parts.working: Fe³⁺ and SO₄²⁻: 2 × (+3) = +6 balances 3 × (−2) = −6. A is iron(II) sulfate.

practice.stem:
Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added drop by drop and then in excess to three solutions taken from a water pipe workshop in Sialkot.
solution J: light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess
solution K: green precipitate, insoluble in excess
solution L: red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the cation present in solution J, solution K and solution L.
parts.answer: J: Cu²⁺; K: Fe²⁺; L: Fe³⁺

parts.label: b
parts.text: The precipitate from solution K slowly turns brown at the surface when left in air. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Iron(II) is oxidised (by oxygen in the air) to iron(III).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of the precipitate in solution J.
parts.answer: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s)
parts.working: B1 correct species and balancing; B1 state symbols.

practice.stem: A student adds 0.50 g of manganese(IV) oxide to aqueous hydrogen peroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
parts.answer: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen, in cm³ at room temperature and pressure, produced when 0.020 mol of hydrogen peroxide decomposes completely. [1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
parts.answer: 240 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the student could show that the manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst at the end of the experiment.
parts.answer: Filter off, wash and dry the solid and weigh it; its mass is the same as at the start.
parts.working: B1 filter, wash, dry; B1 mass unchanged.

practice.stem: Chromium is a transition element used to make stainless steel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the oxidation number of chromium in chromium(III) oxide, Cr₂O₃, and in potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇.
parts.answer: +3 in Cr₂O₃; +6 in K₂Cr₂O₇

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chromium(III) oxide is green and potassium dichromate is orange. State one other general property of transition elements shown by these compounds.
parts.answer: They form coloured compounds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the formula of chromium(III) chloride.
parts.answer: CrCl₃

practice.stem:
Data for four metals:
sodium: melting point 98 °C, density 0.97 g/cm³
potassium: melting point 63 °C, density 0.86 g/cm³
iron: melting point 1538 °C, density 7.87 g/cm³
copper: melting point 1085 °C, density 8.96 g/cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to identify the two transition elements. Give two reasons.
parts.answer: Iron and copper; they have much higher melting points and much higher densities than sodium and potassium.
parts.working: B1 Fe and Cu; B1 high melting points; B1 high densities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why iron (as steel) rather than sodium is used for building bridges.
parts.answer: Iron is strong / hard and does not react with water like sodium does.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Copper(II) sulfate is blue but sodium sulfate is white. Which property of transition elements does this show?
parts.answer: They form coloured compounds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the colour and physical state at room temperature of: (i) chlorine, (ii) bromine, (iii) iodine.
parts.answer: (i) pale yellow-green gas; (ii) red-brown liquid; (iii) grey-black solid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend in density down Group VII.
parts.answer: Density increases down the group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of a chlorine atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the charge on the ion formed by chlorine, and explain why it has this charge.
parts.answer: 1−; the atom gains one electron to get a full outer shell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formulae of the compounds formed when chlorine reacts with (i) magnesium and (ii) hydrogen.
parts.answer: (i) MgCl₂; (ii) HCl

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mixture of aqueous solutions reacts to produce a halogen?
A bromine and potassium chloride
B iodine and potassium bromide
C chlorine and potassium bromide
D iodine and potassium chloride
parts.answer: C chlorine and potassium bromide
parts.working: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its halide: chlorine displaces bromine. In A bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so no reaction.

practice.stem: Chlorine water is added to aqueous potassium iodide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour change seen.
parts.answer: Colourless to brown (orange-brown).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the species that is oxidised. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Iodide ions; they lose electrons (oxidation number goes from −1 to 0).

practice.stem:
Three solutions A, B and C each contain one sodium halide. A student adds dilute nitric acid and then aqueous silver nitrate to each, and in separate tests adds chlorine water.
solution A: white precipitate; no change with chlorine water
solution B: yellow precipitate; solution turns brown with chlorine water
solution C: cream precipitate; solution turns orange with chlorine water

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the halide ion in each solution.
parts.answer: A: chloride (Cl⁻); B: iodide (I⁻); C: bromide (Br⁻)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why chlorine water causes no visible change with solution A.
parts.answer: Chlorine cannot displace chloride (no reaction) — the halogen and halide are the same.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dilute nitric acid is added before the aqueous silver nitrate.
parts.answer: To remove (react with) carbonate ions, which would also give a precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Astatine is below iodine in Group VII. Predict its physical state and colour at room temperature.
parts.answer: solid; black

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether bromine would react with aqueous sodium astatide. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Yes; bromine is more reactive than astatine, so it displaces astatine.
parts.working: B1 yes; B1 bromine more reactive.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of electrons, why the halogens become less reactive down the group.
parts.answer: Atoms get larger with more shells; the outer shell is further from the nucleus (more shielding), so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker and an electron is gained less easily.
parts.working: B1 more shells / larger atoms; B1 weaker attraction of nucleus for outer electrons; B1 less easily gains an electron.

practice.stem:
Melting points of the halogens:
fluorine −220 °C, chlorine −101 °C, bromine −7 °C, iodine 114 °C, astatine ?

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in the melting points of the halogens.
parts.answer: Melting point increases down the group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the melting point of astatine.
parts.answer: Any value from 200 °C to 320 °C
parts.working: The melting point rises by roughly 100–120 °C per element, so about 220–240 °C is expected; accept 200–320 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the trend in melting points in terms of forces.
parts.answer: Molecules get larger down the group, so the intermolecular forces get stronger and more energy is needed to overcome them.
parts.working: B1 larger molecules; B1 stronger intermolecular forces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two observations when a small piece of sodium is added to water.
parts.answer: Any two of: floats; melts into a ball; moves around on the surface; fizzes; gets smaller and disappears.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Universal indicator is added to the solution at the end. Suggest the pH.
parts.answer: about 13–14 (alkaline)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property increases going down Group I from lithium to potassium?
A melting point
B reactivity with water
C number of outer-shell electrons
D hardness
parts.answer: B reactivity with water
parts.working: Reactivity increases down Group I. Melting point and hardness decrease, and the number of outer electrons stays at one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rubidium is below potassium in Group I. Predict how rubidium reacts with water compared with potassium.
parts.answer: More vigorously / faster (may explode).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formula of rubidium oxide and the formula of rubidium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Rb₂O; RbOH

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why rubidium is stored under oil.
parts.answer: To stop it reacting with oxygen and water vapour in the air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: All Group I metals form ions with a 1+ charge. Explain why.
parts.answer: They have one electron in the outer shell, which is lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of atomic structure, why potassium is more reactive than sodium.
parts.answer: Potassium atoms have more shells, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded; it is less strongly attracted and is lost more easily.
parts.working: B1 more shells / larger atom; B1 weaker attraction for outer electron; B1 electron lost more easily.

practice.stem:
0.46 g of sodium reacts completely with water.
2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of sodium used. [Ar: Na = 23]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at room temperature and pressure, in cm³. [1 mol of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.]
parts.answer: 240 cm³
parts.working: M1 0.010 mol H₂ (2Na → H₂); A1 240 cm³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The solution is made up to 250 cm³ with distilled water. Calculate the concentration of sodium hydroxide in mol/dm³.
parts.answer: 0.080 mol/dm³

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Caesium burns in chlorine. Which row correctly describes the product?
A CsCl₂, covalent, insoluble in water
B CsCl, ionic, white solid that dissolves to form a neutral solution
C CsCl, covalent, coloured liquid
D Cs₂Cl, ionic, dissolves to form an alkaline solution
parts.answer: B CsCl, ionic, white solid that dissolves to form a neutral solution
parts.working: Cs⁺ and Cl⁻ give CsCl, an ionic white solid like NaCl; its solution is neutral. D wrongly predicts an alkaline solution, which forms only when the metal reacts with water.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What do elements in the same group of the Periodic Table have in common?
A the same number of electron shells
B the same number of outer-shell electrons
C the same nucleon number
D the same number of neutrons
parts.answer: B the same number of outer-shell electrons
parts.working: Elements in a group have the same number of outer electrons, which is why they have similar chemical properties. A describes elements in the same period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An element has the electronic configuration 2,8,6. State its group and period.
parts.answer: Group VI; Period 3

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the element.
parts.answer: sulfur

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether it is a metal or a non-metal and give the formula of the ion it forms.
parts.answer: non-metal; S²⁻

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the change in metallic character across Period 3 from sodium to argon.
parts.answer: Changes from metals to non-metals (metallic character decreases).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the nature (acidic or basic) of the oxides of elements on the left and on the right of Period 3. Give one example of each.
parts.answer: Left: basic, e.g. Na₂O or MgO; right: acidic, e.g. SO₂ or P₄O₁₀.
parts.working: B1 basic; B1 correct example; B1 acidic; B1 correct example.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An element forms an ion with a 3+ charge. Its atom has three occupied electron shells. Which element is it?
A boron
B aluminium
C gallium
D phosphorus
parts.answer: B aluminium
parts.working: Aluminium (2,8,3) is in Group III and Period 3 and loses 3 electrons. Boron is in Group III but has only two shells.

practice.stem:
Electronic configurations of four elements:
D 2,2
E 2,8,7
F 2,8,8,1
G 2,8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place each element in the Periodic Table by stating its group and period.
parts.answer: D: Group II, Period 2; E: Group VII, Period 3; F: Group I, Period 4; G: Group 0 (VIII), Period 2

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which two elements would react together most vigorously? Give a reason.
parts.answer: F and E; F is a very reactive metal (low in Group I) and E is a reactive non-metal (Group VII), so F gives its electron to E readily.
parts.working: B1 F and E; B1 reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Element X is in Group II and Period 4. Give its electronic configuration and name it.
parts.answer: 2,8,8,2; calcium

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the formula of the compound formed between X and chlorine, and between X and oxygen.
parts.answer: XCl₂ (CaCl₂); XO (CaO)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the type of bonding in the chloride of X. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Ionic; X is a metal that loses two electrons and chlorine is a non-metal that gains an electron.
parts.working: B1 ionic; B1 metal + non-metal / electron transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the noble gases are unreactive.
parts.answer: They have a full outer shell of electrons (stable configuration).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one use of argon and one use of helium, and give the property that makes each suitable.
parts.answer: Argon: filling light bulbs / lamps, because it is unreactive (inert); helium: filling balloons / airships, because it has a low density and is unreactive.
parts.working: B1 argon use; B1 property; B1 helium use; B1 property.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Argon makes up about 0.9 % of air. A student says argon exists as Ar₂ molecules. Explain why this is wrong.
parts.answer: Argon has a full outer shell (2,8,8), so it does not form bonds; it exists as single atoms (monatomic).
parts.working: B1 full outer shell / stable; B1 monatomic, no bonds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the electronic configuration of argon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the group in which the noble gases are found.
parts.answer: Group VIII (Group 0)

practice.stem:
Boiling points of the noble gases:
helium −269 °C, neon −246 °C, argon −186 °C, krypton −153 °C, xenon −108 °C, radon ?

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in boiling points down the group.
parts.answer: Boiling point increases down the group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the boiling point of radon and its state at room temperature.
parts.answer: About −60 °C (any value from −80 °C to −40 °C); gas
parts.working: B1 value in range; B1 gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why boiling point increases down the group.
parts.answer: Atoms are larger (more electrons), so the forces between atoms are stronger and need more energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 larger atoms; B1 stronger forces between atoms.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. What is formed at each electrode?
A cathode: lead; anode: bromine
B cathode: bromine; anode: lead
C cathode: hydrogen; anode: bromine
D cathode: lead; anode: oxygen
parts.answer: A cathode: lead; anode: bromine
parts.working: Positive Pb²⁺ ions move to the cathode and gain electrons to form lead; Br⁻ ions move to the anode and lose electrons to form bromine. B swaps the electrodes; there is no water, so no hydrogen or oxygen can form.

practice.stem: Zinc chloride, ZnCl₂, is an ionic compound with a fairly low melting point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term electrolysis.
parts.answer: The decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by the passage of an electric current.
parts.working: B1 decomposition/breakdown of ionic compound (molten or aqueous); B1 by electricity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the positive electrode.
parts.answer: Anode

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why solid zinc chloride does not conduct electricity but molten zinc chloride does.
parts.answer: In the solid the ions are fixed in a lattice and cannot move; when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.
parts.working: B1 solid: ions cannot move; B1 molten: ions mobile.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the products at the cathode and at the anode when molten zinc chloride is electrolysed.
parts.answer: Cathode: zinc; anode: chlorine

practice.stem: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed using platinum electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gas formed at the cathode and the gas formed at the anode.
parts.answer: Cathode: hydrogen; anode: oxygen

parts.label: b
parts.text: 36 cm³ of gas is collected at the cathode. State the volume of gas collected at the anode in the same time.
parts.answer: 18 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Complete the half-equation for the anode: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + ___ + ___
parts.answer: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻

practice.stem: Concentrated aqueous sodium bromide is electrolysed using carbon electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the four ions present in the solution.
parts.answer: Na⁺, Br⁻, H⁺, OH⁻
parts.working: B1 for Na⁺ and Br⁻; B1 for H⁺ and OH⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product at each electrode.
parts.answer: Cathode: hydrogen; anode: bromine
parts.working: B1 each. Hydrogen, not sodium, because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen; bromide is discharged because the solution is concentrated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what is seen near the anode.
parts.answer: The solution turns orange (yellow-orange / orange-brown) as bromine forms.

practice.stem: A student electrolyses concentrated aqueous sodium chloride in an apparatus that collects the gas from each electrode in a separate tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen at each electrode.
parts.answer: Bubbles of gas at both electrodes; the gas at the anode is pale green / yellow-green.
parts.working: B1 bubbles at both; B1 pale green at anode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student holds damp blue litmus paper at the top of the anode tube. State what happens.
parts.answer: It turns red and then is bleached (white).
parts.working: B1 bleached; accept red then white.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The volume of gas at the anode is a little less than at the cathode, although equal volumes are expected. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Some chlorine dissolves in the water/solution.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the gas formed at the cathode.
parts.answer: Hydrogen

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance conducts electricity when molten but not when solid?
A copper
B sodium chloride
C sulfur
D graphite
parts.answer: B sodium chloride
parts.working: Sodium chloride is ionic: its ions cannot move in the solid but can move when molten. Copper and graphite conduct when solid; sulfur does not conduct in either state.

practice.stem: Name the two products formed when each molten compound is electrolysed with inert electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: molten potassium iodide
parts.answer: Potassium and iodine

parts.label: b
parts.text: molten calcium chloride
parts.answer: Calcium and chlorine

parts.label: c
parts.text: molten aluminium oxide
parts.answer: Aluminium and oxygen

parts.label: d
parts.text: State at which electrode the metal is formed in each case and explain why.
parts.answer: The cathode; metal ions are positive and are attracted to the negative electrode, where they gain electrons.
